source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Cassava green mite, Mononychellus tanajoa, lives on the under surface of young cassava leaves. Mites are wingless, very tiny, and appear as specks to the naked eye. Crop damage symptoms: Cassava green mite sucks sap from cassava leaves and shoot tips. The pest causes tiny yellow chlorotic spots the size of pin pricks on the upper leaf surfaces. Young leaves attacked by cassava green mite become small and narrow. The pest kills the terminal leaves and as these drop the shoot tip looks like a 'candlestick'. Damage is more severe in the dry than in the wet season. Control: the IITA variety TMS 30572 and national varieties 8017 and 8034 in Cameroon, and MS6 and NR 8082 in Nigeria are good against cassava green mite. Predatory mites called phytoseiids, especially Typhlodromalus aripo, are the most effective natural enemy. Farmers should avoid pesticide use on cassava because it kills these natural enemies.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: The cassava mealybug, Phenacoccus manihoti, is commonly found at cassava shoot tips, on the under surfaces of leaves, and on stems, covered with large amounts of white waxy material. It sucks sap from leaves and shoot tips, reduces internode length causing leaves to clump into 'bunchy tops', distorts stems, dries up leaves, and can defoliate plants if severe. Damage is more severe in the dry season. The wasp Apoanagyrus lopezi is the most effective natural enemy and has controlled the pest across most of Africa. Newly hatched mealybugs are tiny and spread by wind and on infested stem cuttings used for planting; farmers should avoid selecting planting material from infested plants.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: The whitefly Bemisia tabaci is a small insect with bright white wings. Adults and nymphs are found on the under-surfaces of young cassava leaves. The nymphs appear as pale yellow oval specks to the naked eye. Whiteflies suck sap from the leaves, but this feeding does not cause visible physical damage to the plant. The real danger is that as they feed, the insects inject the plant with viruses that cause cassava mosaic disease. This virus transmission is the main reason Bemisia whitefly is an important cassava pest. Infected plants show yellow and green leaf mottling, leaf distortion, and stunted growth. The whitefly population builds up rapidly in warm, dry conditions.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: The best way to control pests is to grow a healthy cassava crop rather than simply killing pest organisms. This means combining good plant production practices with plant protection, known as Integrated Pest Management (IPM). At planting time, important IPM practices include site selection, soil improvement, and choosing the right varieties and planting materials. Many cassava pests are spread by carrying and planting infested stem cuttings. The main stem-borne pests are cassava mealybug, cassava green mite, spiraling whitefly, and white scale. These pests survive on cassava stems and leaves and are easily carried to new fields. When selecting planting material, look for plants with robust stems, lush foliage, and minimal stem and leaf damage. Avoid selecting cuttings from plants showing pest damage symptoms. If healthy stems are hard to find, you can lay infested stem cuttings flat and bury them completely in the soil to kill pests on the stem surface, or dip cuttings in a diluted pesticide solution such as Rogor at 1% concentration. Always consult the label for application guidelines and safety precautions. In areas with termite problems, smear the cut ends of stem cuttings with a watery paste of soil mixed with kerosene. When cutting stems into planting pieces, select the middle brown-skinned portions — these sprout better and are more vigorous than the top green stem portions, which dehydrate quickly and are easily damaged by pests. Cassava white scale normally affects only a few plants per farm; destroy infested stems during the growing period and after harvest and do not store them with healthy planting material. Several cassava varieties provide natural pest and disease tolerance. IITA TMS 4(2)1425 has high yield, high dry matter, low cyanogenic potential, good ground storability, good weed suppression, moderate tolerance to cassava green mite and cassava bacterial blight, and good tolerance to cassava mosaic disease. TMS 30572 has high yield, high dry matter, moderate cyanogenic potential, moderate ground storability, good weed suppression, moderate tolerance to cassava green mite, and good tolerance to cassava mosaic disease and cassava bacterial blight. Cameroon's 8017 and 8034 varieties have high yield, high dry matter, moderate cyanogenic potential, and moderate tolerance across all three (cassava green mite, cassava mosaic disease, cassava bacterial blight). Nigeria's MS 6 has high yield, high dry matter, low cyanogenic potential, poor ground storability, poor weed suppression, good tolerance to cassava green mite and cassava bacterial blight, and moderate tolerance to cassava mosaic disease. NR 8082 (Nigeria) has high yield, high dry matter, high cyanogenic potential, moderate ground storability, good weed suppression, and good tolerance to all three: cassava green mite, cassava mosaic disease, and cassava bacterial blight.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Spiraling whitefly: Adults of the spiraling whitefly, Aleurodicus dispersus, are bright white in color. Adults and nymphs of the insect occur in large numbers on the undersurfaces of cassava leaves covered with large amounts of white waxy materials. The spiraling whitefly sucks sap from cassava leaves. As it feeds, it secretes large amounts of honeydew which supports the growth of black mold on the plant. The blackened leaves dry up and drop. After mating, females of the spiraling whitefly lay eggs on the undersurface of leaves. The eggs occur in spiral patterns of white material secreted by the insect on the leaves. The insects are numerous mainly in the dry season. The spiraling whitefly spreads by active flight and by being transported on stem planting materials. In addition to cassava, the spiraling whitefly feeds on many types of fruit trees such as citrus, banana, and plantains, as well as vegetables and ornamental plants.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Variegated grasshopper: Adults of the variegated grasshopper, Zonocerus variegatus, are green and have bold yellow, black, white and orange markings on their bodies. The nymphs are black with yellow markings on the body, legs, antennae and wing pads. The young nymphs gather in large numbers on weeds and low-growing crops. The variegated grasshopper chews cassava leaves, petioles, and green stems. It defoliates the plants and debarks the stems. The pest damage is more common on older than on younger cassava plants, and is more severe in the dry than in the wet season. After mating, female variegated grasshoppers lay many egg pods just below the surface of the soil. The egg pods look like tiny groundnut pods. The egg laying sites always have vegetation which casts shade on the ground and keeps it moist, soft, and suitable for egg laying. These sites are usually close to cassava fields and small in surface area. In most of West and Central Africa, adult grasshoppers can be seen in large numbers at such sites, usually between March and May. The eggs start to hatch at the beginning of the main dry season, usually in October and November. The variegated grasshopper spreads by flying from farm to farm. However, the insect does not fly over long distances. It spreads faster in areas where the forest has been cleared than in thick vegetation.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Cassava root scale: The cassava root scale, Stictococcus vayssierrei, seems to be restricted to parts of Central Africa. The cassava root scale lives underground on the storage roots, feeder roots and submerged stems of cassava. The insects are reddish-purple or brown in color, oval in shape, and look like ticks on cassava. They lack wings and are attached firmly to the plant. Cassava root scale attack causes the storage roots to be smaller than normal and deformed. It is not yet known how the cassava root scale spreads. In addition to cassava, the cassava root scale attacks yam, cocoyam, and groundnut.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Stem and root feeders: The common stem and root pests of cassava are termites, cassava root scale, cassava white scale, and vertebrates. Termites: Many different kinds of termites damage cassava stems and storage roots. Termites live in soil or in nests above the ground. They can also be found in tunnels on the surface of cassava stems. Termite nests contain worker, soldier, queen, and king termites. Worker and soldier termites are the ones you normally see when you break open the nests. The workers and soldiers are small insects with white or brown bodies and brown heads. They may or may not have wings. Worker termites cause all the damage to crops and feed all the other members of the nest. The soldier termites fight off other creatures which may enter or destroy the nest. In newly planted cassava farms termites chew and eat stem cuttings. These grow poorly, die and rot. In older cassava farms, termites chew and enter the stems. This weakens the stems and causes them to break easily. Termite damage occurs mostly in the dry season. King and queen termites produce all the other members of the termite nest. They are always hidden in special chambers in the nests, and you are unlikely to see them. In addition to cassava, termites attack many other crops including maize, yam, and groundnut.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: The plant parts attacked by pests determine how much the farmer loses. Pests which damage the plant parts that you harvest rob you directly of food and income. For example, when cassava storage roots are attacked the plants do not replace them with more roots nor do the roots become bigger to compensate for the damage. Pests which cause this kind of damage are the cassava root scale and vertebrates which feed on the roots. However, when pests attack cassava leaves the plants may produce new leaves and later produce a good root yield. The season of attack matters: many cassava pests are dry season pests. They will cause greater yield loss in cassava planted at the end of the wet season late planting than at the beginning of the season early planting. The frequency of attack also matters: cassava plants usually recover from initial pest attack by producing new leaves. However, the plants may not recover from continued attack by the pest.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Parasitoids are natural enemies that kill insect pests by living and growing inside them. The parasitoids reared and released against cassava pests are mainly tiny wasps which lay their eggs inside the pests. The eggs hatch into larvae which eat the internal tissues of the pest, growing and killing it. The body of the dead pest does not rot but it becomes hard. This hardened body is called a mummy. The larvae grow into adult wasps inside the mummies. Later, tiny wasps emerge from these mummies and kill more pests by laying eggs in them. The wasp Apoanagyrus, also known as Epidinocarsis lopezi, is the most effective natural enemy against the cassava mealybug, and it has controlled the pest in most of Africa. Another tiny wasp, Encarsia haitiensis, is a common natural enemy of the spiraling whitefly. Mummies of the cassava mealybug are brown while those of the spiraling whitefly are black. The wasp used in the biological control of the cassava mealybug prefers mealybugs that are large in size. Large mealybugs are found on vigorously growing cassava plants. Soil improvement practices which promote vigorous cassava plant growth will therefore improve biological control of the mealybug by the wasp. Biological control is safe because natural enemies attack only the pests against which they have been reared and released; they do not attack other insects or plants. Biological control is effective because natural enemies stay on the farm permanently and reproduce quickly to respond to any pest outbreak. Biological control saves farmers the cost of pesticides and avoids the dangers of pesticides which can poison people, livestock, and the environment.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Cultural control of the variegated grasshopper: In any year, the abundance of the variegated grasshopper depends largely on the number of egg pods that survive in the soil during the wet season. The destruction of egg pods will therefore reduce the numbers of the pest. Farmers can locate and mark egg-laying sites early in the wet season. At a later stage they can then dig up the soil at the sites to expose and destroy the egg pods. The digging up of eggs should be done before the eggs start to hatch early in the dry season, for example, in October in most of West Africa. The variegated grasshopper does not lay egg pods deep in the soil. Therefore, it is easy to dig out the egg pods. However, egg pod destruction needs to be carried out over a wide area in the wet season in order to control the pest effectively. This will require the participation of many farmers on many neighboring cassava farms. If only one farmer destroys the eggs in and around his or her farm, the pest will later invade the farm from the neighboring farms and bushes. Extension agents can organize the community of villages to dig up and destroy the egg pods on as many farms as possible. Certain weeds, for example Siam weed Chromolaena odorata, harbor immature stages of the variegated grasshopper. From the weeds the pest will move onto cassava plants. You can therefore discourage the pests from gathering in your farm by removing these weeds in your farm. Vertebrate pests of cassava are usually difficult to control. A number of cultural practices will however help to reduce the damage caused by these pests: make good seedbeds for planting cassava so that the storage roots will not be easily exposed later on; if the storage roots are exposed, cover them with soil to prevent them from being attacked and eaten by birds and rodents; fence farms to prevent entry by grasscutters, cattle, sheep, and goats; set traps in the fence against grasscutters and other rodents; weed cassava farms on time and slash weeds and vegetation around the farm to discourage grasscutters and other rodents; organize the village community to hunt for grasscutters in your area; grow bitter cassava varieties where pigs and monkeys are a severe problem as pigs and monkeys prefer sweet cassava varieties; harvest cassava storage roots as soon as they are mature to reduce the length of time they can be exposed and damaged by the pests.

source_title: Pest Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: To control pests and grow a healthy crop of cassava: identify the common pests, their damage symptoms, and natural enemies correctly, and know the conditions under which the pests will cause severe losses. Select sites with dense vegetation, deep loamy soils, and flat or gently sloping land to plant cassava. Improve the soils by manuring, mulching, and intercropping. Grow cassava varieties that tolerate the common pests in your area. Plant healthy stem cuttings or treat the stem cuttings against pest damage; avoid transporting and planting cassava stems infested with stem-borne pests; after harvesting, destroy cassava stems infested with stem-borne pests. Plant cassava mainly at the beginning of the wet season and avoid late planting. Use natural enemies against cassava pests. Do not spray pesticides on cassava as these will kill the natural enemies of cassava pests. Dig egg-laying sites of the variegated grasshopper in the wet season to expose and destroy egg pods of the pest. In the control of bird, rodent, and other vertebrate pests of cassava, fence farms and set traps in the fence; cover exposed storage roots with soil; organize villages to hunt for grasscutters; weed your cassava farm on time to discourage rodent pests; and harvest cassava storage roots as soon as they are mature.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: Anthracnose is caused by the fungus Colletotrichum lindemuthianum. The pathogen is widely distributed, being present in almost all areas where beans are grown. Isolates from cowpea have been obtained from Nigeria and other parts of Africa, India, and Brazil. The disease is particularly severe in monocropped cowpeas in which it can cause up to 50 percent loss in yield. All above-ground parts can be affected but anthracnose is chiefly a stem disease in cowpea. Individual lesions are lenticular to sunken, and tan to brown in color. Lesion size and distribution depend on varietal susceptibility. Highly susceptible lines develop large spreading lesions which rapidly merge to girdle stems, branches, peduncles, and petioles. Anthracnose can be distinguished from scab by the presence of black setae. Primary inoculum may come from seed, with about 40 percent seed transmission, or from diseased plant debris. Secondary spread is rapid during cool, wet weather. The disease may be controlled by using clean seed, application of benomyl or mancozeb at 0.2 percent a.i., or by growing resistant varieties. Pathogenic variants occur.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: Seedling mortality is caused by Pythium aphanidermatum and Corticium solani, also known as Rhizoctonia solani or Thanatephorus cucumeris. The causal fungi are ubiquitous. Seedling mortality has been investigated in Nigeria but the disease probably occurs elsewhere. Seventy-five percent mortality of cowpea seedlings has been obtained within 21 days after sowing. Disease incidence is highest during cool, wet, overcast weather. Both pre-emergence and post-emergence mortality occur; in the latter case, symptoms can be observed on the hypocotyls. The reddish brown lesions caused by C. solani are usually limited to the collar region of the hypocotyl at which point the diseased seedling topples. P. aphanidermatum, however, moves rapidly up the hypocotyl giving it a grey-green, wet appearance and the seedlings undergo a watery collapse. These pathogens are abundant in the soils in the forest region of southern Nigeria where the humid environment is favorable for their activity. Seedling mortality is effectively controlled with chloroneb, also known as demosan, applied as a seed dressing at 2 grams per kilogram of seed.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: The pod sucking bug Nezara viridula, commonly known as the green stink bug, is widespread in the tropics and subtropics. It is primarily a pest of soybean, but also does extensive damage to cowpea crops. Batches of 30 to 80 eggs are laid on the underside of the leaves. A single female may lay from 100 to 250 eggs in four to six batches. There are five nymphal instars. Nymphs are shiny with bright spots. Adults are green and triangular in shape. The entire life cycle may take 30 to 60 days. Both adults and nymphs suck the sap from the developing pods causing damage similar to that caused by Anoplocnemis curvipes.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: The pod sucking bug Anoplocnemis curvipes is a major pest in tropical Africa; yield losses vary from 30 to 70 percent. Full grown bugs are black and are about 3 centimeters long. Eggs are laid in chains and are grey to black. They hatch in about 7 to 11 days. There are five nymphal instars, and the early instars resemble ants. The total nymphal period varies from 29 to 54 days; the life of an adult from 24 to 84 days. Eggs are usually laid on leguminous trees or weeds, but seldom on cowpeas. Adults are strong fliers. They suck the sap from green pods, causing them to shrivel and dry prematurely with resulting loss of seed.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: The cowpea seed moth, Cydia ptychora, also known as Laspeyresia ptychora, is a widely distributed and locally important pest of cowpea in tropical Africa. Cydia species also infest soybean and lima bean in Asia and Latin America as well as Africa. The adult moth is tiny and dull brown or black. The females lay eggs mostly on the nearly mature peduncles or pods. The first instar larvae enter the pod and feed on the seeds remaining inside the pod. Early instar larvae are whitish, but later instars are pink to bright red. They pupate in the soil.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: The legume pod borer, Maruca testulalis, is widely distributed throughout the tropics and subtropics where it may cause extreme damage. It is a major cowpea pest in Africa and Southeast Asia. The adult is a nocturnal moth, light brown with whitish markings on its forewings. The larva is light brown with irregular brown-black dorsal, lateral and ventral spots and a black head. Adult moths live for up to a week and lay eggs on leaf buds, flower buds, and in flowers. Eggs hatch in about 5 days and the larvae feed on tender parts of the stem, peduncles, flower buds, flowers, and pods. The characteristic signs of larval feeding are webbing of flowers, pods, and leaves and production of frass on pods. The spatial separation of pods is important; points of contact between pods, and between pods and leaves are especially prone to damage. About 150 eggs are laid per female. There are five larval instars which together last 8 to 11 days before pupation.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: The foliage beetle, Ootheca mutabilis, is widely distributed in Africa where it is an important foliage feeder on cowpea seedlings. In East Africa a related species, O. bennigseni, is also found. Adults are about 6 millimeters long, oval, and normally shiny reddish brown, although this varies considerably and black or brown adults may occur. Yellow egg masses are laid in soil, and there are three larval instars. Adults feed interveinally on the leaves, later enlarging damage into feeding holes. High beetle populations can totally defoliate cowpea seedlings and kill them. The larvae feed on cowpea roots but seldom cause serious damage. Adult beetles are effective vectors of cowpea yellow mosaic virus.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: Leafhoppers, Empoasca species, are widely distributed in the tropics and subtropics. Important species include E. kerri in Asia, E. dolichi in Africa, and E. kraemeri in Central and South America. The biology of the several species of Empoasca is generally similar. Eggs are laid on the underside of leaves and hatch into nymphs within 7 to 10 days. There are five stages in nymphal development which last about 10 days before the adult appears. The adults' life expectancy varies from 30 to 60 days. Leafhoppers infest cowpeas at the seedling stage. The symptoms of damage are yellow discoloration of the leaf veins and margins, followed by cupping of the leaves. Severely infested plants become stunted, leading to confusion with virus symptoms and may dry prematurely. Cowpea cultivars resistant to Empoasca have been identified.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: Pythium stem rot is caused by Pythium aphanidermatum. It is found worldwide. In Nigeria, field incidence in cowpea normally ranges between 0.5 and 10.0 percent, although occasional incidences of up to 30 percent have been observed. Pythium stem rot is characterized by a grey-green water-soaked girdle of the stem extending from soil level up to and sometimes including the lower portions of the lower branches. During periods of high humidity copious growth of white, cottony mycelia occurs at the stem base. Infected plants quickly wilt and die. The presence of oospores of the causal fungus in the stem cortical tissue distinguishes this disease from Sclerotium stem rot and Fusarium collar rot which superficially resemble it. Cowpea stem rot caused by Phytophthora species, fungi closely related to Pythium, is of local importance in North America, Australia, and India. The disease is probably not seed-transmitted and is principally soil-borne. Bi-weekly applications of captafol effectively control the disease, but benomyl may increase its incidence.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: Black spot, also known as leaf smut, is caused by the fungus Protomycopsis phaseoli, also known as Entyloma vignae. The taxonomy of the causal fungus is controversial. P. phaseoli is widely distributed on cowpeas in tropical Africa and Jamaica, and on cowpeas, beans, and other legumes in India and Nepal. The disease is of major economic importance on cowpea in Brazil where yield losses of 30 to 40 percent are reported. Dark ash-grey to sooty-black circular discrete leaf spots 6 to 8 mm in diameter, surrounded by narrow yellow haloes, are characteristic symptoms. The leaf spots enlarge to 10 mm or more, becoming greenish-grey, irregular and diffuse; severe infections cause premature defoliation. The presence of thick-walled, dark and warty chlamydospores in infected tissue is diagnostic. The chlamydospores survive in plant debris for at least two years but lose their viability when buried. The fungus is not seed-borne. Control measures include rotation, destruction of crop residues, and the use of fungicides. Resistant varieties have been identified in Brazil.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: False rust, also known as yellow blister, is caused by the fungus Synchytrium dolichi. It is widespread on cowpeas in tropical Africa and Asia where it is of minor, local importance. False rust usually develops late in the development of the crop but can be damaging in some areas like Uganda. The first symptoms are pinhead yellow blisters, slightly greasy in appearance, which rapidly spread to cover leaves, petioles, peduncles, pods, and stems. Later the blisters burst, releasing orange-brown sporangia, ultimately leading to the development of raised warty orange-brown scabs. The disease often causes considerable distortion of the plant. The pathogen is probably not seed transmitted. False rust may be controlled by destruction of crop residues, rotation, and by mancozeb sprays.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: Pink rust is caused by the fungus Phakopsora pachyrhizi. P. pachyrhizi is widely distributed in Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean on soybean, cowpea, and other legumes. It appears to be of minor importance on cowpea, though early infection causes premature defoliation. The disease is more damaging during the rainy seasons in southern Nigeria. Lower leaf surfaces bear numerous pinkish-tan colored, conical, protruding pustules which contain colorless uredospores; angular lesions occur on upper leaf surfaces. Pink rust may be confused with bacterial pustule in the field, and microscopic examination may be helpful. Pink rust lesions are neither greasy like bacterial pustule nor powdery like brown rust. The pathogen survives on infected volunteer plants and on alternate hosts. P. pachyrhizi is probably not internally seed-borne. Various chemicals have been effectively used as sprays and seed treatments, including benomyl, maneb, mancozeb, and zineb. Varieties differ in susceptibility and P. pachyrhizi is pathogenically variable.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: Web blight is caused by the fungus Corticium solani, also known as Rhizoctonia solani or Thanatephorus cucumeris. It occurs worldwide and the pathogen is probably present in all arable soils. Web blight of cowpea is especially prevalent in the humid forest belt of West Africa where the disease can totally destroy the crop during periods of heavy rain. Initial symptoms on the leaves are small, circular reddish-brown spots which enlarge, becoming surrounded by irregular shaped water-soaked areas. Under humid conditions, the lesions develop rapidly and coalesce, and mycelium of C. solani can be clearly observed on the undersurface of leaves and on young stems. The initial discrete leaf lesions may be confused with those induced by Cercospora canescens, but the subsequent spreading lesions are characteristic of web blight. The pathogen survives as sclerotia in soil and on crop residues and weed hosts. Inoculum, which can be seed-borne, is primarily from soil splashed onto basal leaves during heavy rain. Control measures include the use of clean seed and cultural methods such as avoidance of dense plantings and sowing timed to avoid favorable conditions for the disease.

source_title: Cowpea Pests and Diseases (IITA)
excerpt_text: Root knot nematodes, including Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, and M. arenaria, are serious pests of cowpea. All three species of nematode are widespread throughout the tropics. M. incognita can cause severe crop loss. M. javanica may make cowpea more susceptible to fusarium wilt. Affected plants die prematurely as a result of extensive damage to the root system, which may be heavily galled. Root knot galls are easily distinguished from the nodules containing Rhizobium, which are usually small, spherical, and pink inside. Numerous species of non-gall-forming nematodes are also parasitic on cowpeas throughout the subtropics and tropics. The nematodes survive in soil and on alternate hosts. Nematocides are available but uneconomic. Crop rotation may be effective but the host range may be wide. Sources of host plant resistance are available in cowpea but often are race-specific.

source_title: Disease Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Cassava mosaic disease is caused by a virus which occurs inside cassava leaves and stems. The leaves of cassava plants with the disease are discolored with patches of normal green color mixed with light green, yellow, and white areas. This discoloration is known as chlorosis. The chlorotic patches can be confused with cassava green mite feeding damage. When cassava mosaic attack is severe, the leaves are very small and distorted and the plants are stunted. The disease symptoms are more pronounced on younger plants, usually under 6 months, than on older plants. The main sources of the virus are cassava plants with the disease and the whitefly. The virus occurs in the saliva of the whitefly; during feeding, the insect injects saliva containing the virus into cassava leaves. The virus multiplies and occurs in large numbers in the leaves and stems. Cassava mosaic disease is also spread by planting stem cuttings from plants infected with the disease.

source_title: Disease Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Cassava bacterial blight is caused by a bacterium which occurs inside cassava leaves and stems. Initially, damage by cassava bacterial blight appears as water-soaked dead spots or lesions. The lesions occur between leaf veins and are most evident on the lower surfaces of the leaves. The lesions are small, not completely round in shape, and have a few angles at their edges. These angular lesions later join together into larger patches, killing the leaf blade as they enlarge. The leaf blade turns brown with the water-soaked area at the leading edge of the brown patch, a symptom known as leaf blighting. Severely blighted leaves wilt, die, and fall, causing defoliation and shoot tip die-back or complete death of the shoot. Leaf blighting starts from the leaf blade and moves towards the petiole; the petiole retains a horizontal position before leaf fall. This differs from cassava anthracnose-damaged leaves whose petioles droop before leaf fall. Drops of brownish gum may occur on the leaves, petioles, and stems of plants infected with cassava bacterial blight. The damage symptoms are more evident in the wet season than in the dry season. The disease is more severe in young plants than in older ones. The main sources of the bacterium are cassava plants with the disease. The bacterium enters plants through wounds and scratches on the stems and leaves, multiplying in large numbers. The disease is spread by planting stem cuttings from plants with disease symptoms, and by raindrops that splash the bacterium from infected plants to healthy ones. Insects such as grasshoppers can become contaminated and spread it. Farm tools used to cut infected plants should be cleaned after use.

source_title: Disease Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Cassava leaf spot diseases are caused by fungi and come in three types: white leaf spot, brown leaf spot, and leaf blight. Cassava white leaf spot disease appears as circular white or brownish-yellow spots on the upper leaf surfaces, sometimes with purplish borders around them. Cassava brown leaf spot disease appears as small brown spots with dark borders on the upper leaf surfaces, occurring between leaf veins with sizes and shapes limited by the distance between veins. The dead tissue in the center of brown spots may fall, giving the leaf surface a shot-hole appearance. Under severe attack, infected leaves turn yellow, dry, and die prematurely. Cassava leaf blight disease appears as light brown lesions on the upper surfaces of the leaves that are not limited by veins and are therefore larger than brown leaf spots. The lesions may enlarge to cover most of the leaf surface and cause leaf blight. Blighted leaves lack water-soaked areas that are typical of leaf damage by cassava bacterial blight. Leaf blight lesions also lack the dark borders of brown leaf spots and do not develop into shot holes on the leaf surface. The main sources of the leaf spot fungi are infected cassava leaves on the plant or those fallen on the ground. The fungi spread to new plants from these sources by wind or rain splashes and can occur on weeds that then serve as sources of the diseases.

source_title: Disease Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Cassava brown streak disease is caused by a virus and is reported from cassava-growing regions in East and Southern Africa. Damage symptoms appear on the leaves, stems, and storage roots of cassava plants. On the leaves, the disease appears as patches of yellow areas mixed with normal green color, which are more prominent on mature leaves than on young leaves. The damaged leaves do not become distorted in shape as occurs with leaves damaged by cassava mosaic disease. On the stems, the disease appears as dark brown streaks with dead spots on leaf scars, most prominent on the upper green portions of the stems. Diseased plants may show shoot tip die-back. Cassava brown streak disease distorts the shape of the storage roots and may cause cracks and discoloration in the storage roots visible when they crack open or are cut. The main sources of the virus are cassava plants with the disease. The disease is spread through the planting of stem cuttings from diseased plants. The virus is also believed to be spread from plant to plant by insects.

source_title: Disease Control in Cassava Farms (IITA IPM Field Guide)
excerpt_text: Cassava root rot diseases are caused by various kinds of fungi that live on or in the soil. The fungi occur mainly in soils that do not drain properly and in forest fallow land that has been recently cleared. The leaves on affected cassava plants turn brown, wilt, and the plant appears scorched. The leaves may or may not remain attached to the plant, but the plant loses a lot of water and dies. To confirm root rot disease, uproot the plant and examine the roots for damage symptoms. Root rot diseases kill both feeder and storage roots of cassava. The storage roots may swell unusually and develop light brown coloration visible if the roots crack open or are cut. The roots may give off a bad smell as they rot. The important sources of cassava root rot fungi are contaminated soils and cassava root and stem debris. The fungi enter plants through wounds caused by pests or farming tools, or by piercing the roots directly. Farm tillage tools used in fields with the disease should be cleaned after use to prevent spreading. Cassava plant debris in affected farms also serves as a source of root rot fungi and should be destroyed by burning.

source_title: PICS hermetic storage bags ineffective in controlling infestations of Prostephanus truncatus and Dinoderus spp. in traditional cassava chips
excerpt_text: The collected data showed that chips stored in PICS bags had a moisture content below 13%, levels considered to be safe for storage and sustaining quality of cassava chips (Gnonlonfin et al., 2008b). The spike in moisture obtained in the WPP bags at 2 months could be related to higher ambient relative humidity observed during the first four weeks of the trial. The rainy season was setting in and since these bags are not airtight this would have directly resulted in an increase in moisture levels. Moisture levels of the stored cassava chips were adequate for insect development and could have affected the chips susceptibility to insect damage. Higher moisture content would lead to softness in chip texture facilitating tunneling by pests. Environmental parameters in the storage room were conducive for the development of P. truncatus, with optimal conditions for the development of this species described at 27 C and 70-80% r.h. (Subramanyam and Hagstrum, 1991) similar to the climatic conditions in the storage room. PICS bags are hermetic storage bags and the basic principle of hermetic storage is the reduction of oxygen levels to levels that suppress or deactivate the capacity of insects, pests, and fungi to reproduce and/or develop (Villers et al., 2010). However, in our trial hermetic storage was probably not achieved, since measured O2 levels of 17% and 4% CO2. In hermetic storage, insects die when the O2 content in the air is reduced to 3% or less (Moreno et al., 2000), feeding will cease when O2 drops below 4% (Murdock et al., 2012).

source_title: Chemical Intervention on All Stages and All Scales of Tropical Storage Practice (Singh, IITA Proceedings)
excerpt_text: Grains need protection from stored grain pests at all stages from field to consumption. In the tropics field to storage infestation by stored grain pests is common. Sitotroga cerealella and Sitophilus oryzae both are primary stored grain pests of rice and they commonly infest paddy in the field before harvest. Similarly Sitophilus zeamais infests maize, Rhyzopertha dominica infests wheat and other cereals and Callosobruchus maculatus infests cowpeas. All these are major stored grain pests. The initial field infestation is carried over to drying and storage. Grains harvested in semi-humid tropics have high moisture level. Maize may have up to 30 percent moisture at harvest at Ibadan, Nigeria. Usually with the subsistence farmer, grains are left near the field for sun drying. During this process insect infestation continues to build up. Cribs made of plant material are used for storing husked and unhusked maize. These materials provide aeration facilities to avoid mould, but at the same time facilitate infestation from surrounding areas. Infestation during drying in cribs and structures is best avoided by cleaning these storage places and dusting with about 1.0 percent lindane dust applied at 10 to 12 ppm. This method is practiced in Africa to a limited extent by subsistence farmers in the case of maize drying and storage. This method is inexpensive but the farmer has to wait 6 to 8 weeks before consumption. Lindane dust is easily available to the farmers. Le Pelley and Kockum recorded that after shelling the lindane residue in maize was reduced to a level of 1 ppm or less when applied as a 1 percent dust at 12 ppm to ears of maize and sorghum. This treatment was found particularly effective in killing and preventing successful egg laying by Sitophilus spp. and Sitotroga cerealella. However resistance to lindane has recently been reported from Malawi and Zambia for Tribolium castaneum and Sitophilus zeamais. Due to reports on lindane resistance, considerable research has been initiated to find out suitable replacements. Iodofenphos, Gardona, fenitrothion, pirimiphosmethyl, phoxim and bromophos are being tested at several field stations in the tropics.

source_title: Growing Cassava: A Training Manual from Production to Postharvest (Abass, Towo, Mukuka, Okechukwu, Ranaivoson, Tarawali, Kanju, IITA)
excerpt_text: Cassava roots are heaped under shade and watered everyday. Undamaged roots are stored in pits or trenches dug in well-drained, sloping and shaded areas. The trenches, with the long side directed downhill, are lined with straw and dried leaves before roots are arranged in them, after which the roots are covered with soil, preferably river-sand or sea-sand. Water-logged areas and heavy clay for covering should be avoided. Cassava roots are coated with clay or mud. Freshly harvested or peeled roots are stored for 1 to 2 days by completely submerging in water. Storage by heaping or soaking, in pits, or by coating extends the shelf life of the roots by only 2 to 3 days and is not suitable for commercial operations. To reduce postharvest losses, harvest when the soil is wet or loose, cut the roots from the stem leaving 2 to 5 cm of the stump on the roots, avoid bruises or damage to the roots during harvesting and transportation, and select uninjured roots if storage of more than 1 week is desired. Treat unpeeled roots with fungicides before storage. For improved storage, select a well-drained area, preferably shaded and slightly sloping. Dig trenches measuring 1 meter wide and 30 to 40 cm deep, with the length directed downhill. At the lower end of the trench, make a drainage ditch at least 20 cm wide and 5 to 10 cm deeper than the storage trench. Arrange mature, undamaged roots inside the trench, covering each layer with soil, preferably river-sand or sea-sand. Clay-loam soil can also be used if it is not too wet. Do not use heavy clay and do not keep cassava in a waterlogged area because roots will rot easily. For storage in sawdust, select healthy roots that were not damaged or bruised and were harvested no longer than 24 hours. Put a layer of damp sawdust in wooden crates or baskets lined with plastic foils, arrange the roots in alternate layers of damp sawdust, and store. To avoid microbial spoilage, the sawdust must be damp, not too wet.

source_title: Growing Cassava: A Training Manual from Production to Postharvest (Abass, Towo, Mukuka, Okechukwu, Ranaivoson, Tarawali, Kanju, IITA)
excerpt_text: A 2-row planter can plant 7 to 10 hectares in 1 day, depending on the terrain. Depending on the type of planter, cassava stems are usually cut into 20 to 25 cm long stakes or cuttings which are planted horizontally, inclined, or vertically. Generally farmers plant by hand and it takes 8 to 10 persons to plant 1 hectare in 1 day. Cassava planting can be mechanized using tractor-powered planters. Mechanical planters are suitable for large-scale planting. For small- or medium-scale farmers, hiring a mechanical planter and paying a fee for planting could be more cost-effective. It is faster and 50% less expensive than planting by hand. The planter requires a tractor of 60 to 70 hp, especially in soils likely to become compacted. Four people are often required to operate a 2-row planter: a tractor driver, two people to feed the stakes into the planter, and one person on the ground. The cuttings need to be the same length, size, and shape with cleanly cut ends. Stem cuttings could be prepared by hand using simple tools such as hacksaws or a small motorized chain saw. A cassava stem cutting machine has also been developed. Some mechanical planters can simultaneously cut cassava stems to stakes of constant length, plant at equidistance, apply fertilizer, and cover the planted stakes. Generally this type of mechanical planter can plant 3 to 6 hectares in 1 day.

source_title: Smallholder Chicken Production Manual (CGIAR/ICRISAT)
excerpt_text: Choose a suitable location for a chicken farm. The location is crucial for the business success. Infrastructure considerations include transport for input supply and product marketing, power and water supply, market availability, and sufficient space for housing the chickens and subsidiary structures. Labor availability depends on the operation size and level of technology use, including both numbers and skill level. Climatic conditions matter: temperatures above 30 degrees Celsius can negatively impact productivity and may require additional investment for climatic control. For biosecurity, locate the farm as far away from other chicken farms as possible.

source_title: Smallholder Chicken Production Manual (CGIAR/ICRISAT)
excerpt_text: Profits equal revenue minus expenditure, so to increase profits a business must decrease costs and increase sales. Farmers need entrepreneurship skills to plan, select enterprises, budget, and analyse costs and benefits. Accurate record-keeping is essential, and seeking help from development agents for professional assistance is recommended. Cost saving measures include reducing or avoiding unnecessary costs, avoiding wastages such as feed waste, and using the right breed for the type of management. Specialized layer breeds are more efficient for intensively managed production than dual-purpose breeds. Applying appropriate biosecurity and disease prevention measures reduces mortality losses and low production due to diseases. Income enhancement strategies include producing good-quality products that can be sold at better prices, promoting products for selling at better-paying markets, reducing marketing costs such as transport, and reducing product loss such as egg breakage. For financial management, keep an accurate daily record of finances in a cash book to track where money comes from and where it goes. Regularly analyse production costs to identify areas where expenses can be reduced and efficiency improved. Monitor costs such as feed costs, labour costs, veterinary services, and energy expenses. Explore opportunities to optimize resource allocation and negotiate better prices with suppliers. Put money in savings regularly, setting aside a small amount each day rather than waiting until the end of the month. Minimize selling products or services on credit and allowing too many long-standing debts, as credit that is not paid is not a sale.

source_title: Smallholder Chicken Production Manual (CGIAR/ICRISAT)
excerpt_text: When constructing a chicken house, use locally available, durable, easy-to-clean, and cost-effective materials, avoiding sharp-edged objects to prevent injury to chickens and humans. Orient the house with the narrow sides facing east and west and the long sides facing north and south for reduced direct sunlight and solar heat and increased bird densities. A rectangular shape provides better natural ventilation, with the length determined by the number and age of chickens and available land. The width should not exceed 9 meters for adequate natural ventilation, especially in hot weather. The roof should be 2.5 to 3.5 meters above ground, or higher in warmer climates, and split in very hot temperatures at 25 and 40 degree angles. The foundation should be made of solid concrete blocks or bricks, set 30 to 45 cm below and above ground level. A concrete floor is preferred for disease control, easy cleaning, and prevention of insect, rodent, worm, and seepage issues. Extend the floor base 45 cm outside the wall to deter rodents. At least two sidewalls should be open, with the lower portion solid and the upper part fitted with small-gauge half-inch wire netting to prevent the entry of birds, cats, and rodents. Providing openings or low-built walls about 1 meter in height, maximum 1.5 meters, provides sufficient ventilation without exposing chickens to draft at bird level. Open sides can be closed with suitable material during colder periods. The roof should be rainproof, thatched for small farms or made of iron sheets and wood. Eaves should extend 1 to 1.25 meters out from the roof, or longer in areas with heavy rainfall. Lighting should be hung from the ceiling at 220 to 250 cm above ground level. Incandescent bulbs should have a distance of 300 cm between them, while fluorescent tube lights should have a gap of 450 cm between them. Accessory structures should include an entrance change room for attendants to change clothing, disinfect shoes, and wash hands before entering the house, a feed store with enough space for one week of feed, and a washbasin for cleaning equipment like drinkers with proper closed drainage.

source_title: Smallholder Chicken Production Manual (CGIAR/ICRISAT)
excerpt_text: The housing and equipment required depend on the production objectives, the number of chickens housed, and the production system used. Extensive chicken houses provide shelter and nesting spaces while allowing chickens to roam freely and scavenge for feed in a larger designated area. The outdoor area may be enclosed with fences to protect the chickens from predators. This system promotes natural behaviours and is often used for organic or free-range production. Semi-intensive chicken houses combine free-range and confinement housing. The run system is an enclosed area with fences 1.5 to 2 meters high for scavenging and exercise, with egg nests, feed, and water provided in the shed or house. The top can be covered with mesh wire or local materials for protection. A moveable house is a low-cost shed that accommodates free-range chickens and provides night shelter. It is equipped with nests and perches, and birds can access surrounding fields during the day for scavenging. This system is suitable for peri-urban areas and can be integrated into cropping by moving chickens around within blocks of open land. Intensive chicken houses confine chickens indoors for their entire lives and require more investment in housing and facilities. Open houses have two open sides and a roof overhang to protect chicks from rain and sun, using wire mesh for the sides in warm or hot areas. Open front houses have only one side open and are suitable for temperatures ranging from 15 to 30 degrees Celsius. Curtain houses have adjustable curtains on both sides for climate control, with maximum curtain opening depending on the local climate: ideally 1.5 meters in warm areas and 0.3 to 0.6 meters in cold areas.

source_title: Smallholder Chicken Production Manual (CGIAR/ICRISAT)
excerpt_text: Clean the chicken house immediately after evacuating the birds to prevent the accumulation and spread of disease-causing agents. Step 1: Remove all organic matter by taking out all the litter from the entrance and disposing of it as far away from the houses as possible. If the litter is used in the fields, work it into the soil to prevent recontamination. Remove all feeders, drinkers, and equipment, wash and disinfect them, soak the feeders and drinkers in disinfectant for a few hours, then rinse with water and expose to sunlight. Step 2: Perform dry cleaning by making necessary repairs to the house and equipment, dusting down the roof, walls, and floor in that order, then sweeping the chicken house, and carefully wiping off any dust from lighting after the light bulbs have cooled down. Step 3: Wash all surfaces of the house thoroughly using a detergent, ensuring that water drains out of the chicken house and entrance. Step 4: Disinfect by cleaning the entire house using a suitable sprayer and a registered disinfectant proven to kill chicken pathogens. Seek professional advice on selecting appropriate disinfectants. Prioritize safety when using disinfectants by following professional recommendations and wearing safety materials such as coveralls, goggles, rubber gloves, rubber boots, a waterproof hat, and a respirator or mask. If these items are unavailable, use local alternatives. Begin with weaker chemicals and gradually increase strength according to the disinfectant producer's recommendations, reading the label and instructions before application. Allow the house to dry and remain closed for as long as possible, two weeks or more, before introducing new chickens. After one day, apply lime to the floor and short walls of the house. Place foot baths or boot dips containing disinfectant at the entrance of each chicken house, and all individuals entering must dip their footwear every time.

source_title: A Comprehensive Training Module on Competitive Cassava Production (IITA)
excerpt_text: Crops continually remove large amounts of nutrients from the soil. Soil destruction through erosion and the removal of nutrients from the topsoil by leaching reduce soil fertility more quickly. Therefore, nutrient supplies need to be put back naturally or by chemical methods through sound soil and crop management practices. What makes a soil fertile? A fertile soil has large amounts of topsoil; is rich in macronutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, sulphur) and micronutrients (boron, cobalt, copper, iron, manganese, molybdenum, zinc); has acidity or alkalinity between pH 6.0 and 7.5; has large amounts of organic matter which improve soil structure and nutrient and moisture retention; has good drainage and aeration; and has soil organisms that enhance the availability of nutrients for plant growth.

source_title: A Comprehensive Training Module on Competitive Cassava Production (IITA)
excerpt_text: You can grow cassava using zero input technology. This does not need chemicals such as fertilizers and herbicides, or organic compost. The zero input method encourages biological activity in the soil and provides natural protection from diseases. It can guarantee good yields, provided that farmers prepare the land well, use the right varieties, plant at the right spacing and time, and ensure a weed-free farm. Zero input technology is meant to inform resource-poor farmers about what they can do to get a good yield when they lack capital to purchase inputs. It focuses on how farmers can use their agronomic skills to achieve high yields, and it proves that the use of chemical inputs is not the only way to promote a good yield.

source_title: A Comprehensive Training Module on Competitive Cassava Production (IITA)
excerpt_text: To use zero input technology for a good cassava yield, choose a good soil with medium fertility and good drainage, avoiding stony, clayey, or water-logged soils. Use a site that has been well maintained. Practice minimum tillage in sandy soils to conserve organic matter and moisture and to reduce soil erosion. Avoid shallow and hard soils, or alternatively make ridges or mounds to increase the topsoil volume per plant for better establishment. Choose improved varieties with the highest and most stable performance in different locations. Select planting materials from healthy cassava plants 10 to 12 months old without stem and leaf damage from pests and diseases. Handle the stems carefully to avoid bruising or damaging the nodes and to improve sprouting. Cut the middle stems into 25 cm lengths with 5 to 7 nodes; middle portions establish better than the tips and basal parts. Plant at the right time to ensure healthy sprouting and good crop establishment. Dry season planting is not recommended when the rains stop early or where the water table is low, because there will not be enough moisture to allow sprouting and the stems to survive. In general, cassava should be planted when 2 months of soil moisture is expected after planting. Plant at the correct spacing: the recommended planting space is 1 m by 0.8 m for non-branching types and 1 m by 1 m for branching types.

source_title: A Comprehensive Training Module on Competitive Cassava Production (IITA)
excerpt_text: Improved cassava varieties grow fast, tolerate major diseases and pests, mature early, give high root yields in both fresh and dry weight, meet end-users' quality needs, and store well in the ground for 12 to 15 months. High yielding and healthy planting materials can be obtained from the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture in Ibadan, Oyo State; the National Root Crops Research Institute in Abia State; state offices of the National Seed Council of Nigeria; state offices of Agricultural Development Programs; state offices of the Cassava Growers Association; and the Roots and Tubers Expansion Programme in Ogun State.

source_title: Climate Risk Management in Agricultural Extension for Ethiopia, 2nd Edition (CGIAR)
excerpt_text: Climate is among the most important drivers of agricultural risk, particularly in rainfed sub-humid to arid environments. Farmers are affected by stochastic variability, meaning randomness from sources such as climate and market prices. Risk refers to the impacts of stochastic variability on productivity, profitability, or some aspect of wellbeing. In the context of climate, a hazard, shock, or extreme event refers to a climate-related physical phenomenon that has the potential to trigger adverse impacts on human wellbeing, directly or through the natural resource base. A stress refers to a condition that can lead to adverse impacts but that occurs over a longer period than a shock. Compound risk refers to instances when multiple types of simultaneous hazards interact. Exposure refers to the frequency and severity of environmental shocks or stresses that a community experiences. Vulnerability refers to characteristics of human communities or social systems that cause them to be susceptible to adverse impacts, such as increased food insecurity, poverty, or mortality, when exposed to an external shock or stress. Resilience refers to the capacity of an individual, community, or society to resist moving to a less desirable state such as poverty, or to recover if it is already in an undesirable state, in the face of stochastic shocks or long-term stresses. Coping refers to the actions that individuals or communities take to withstand a shock and limit its immediate adverse impacts, although some coping strategies reduce livelihood opportunities or increase vulnerability in the long term. Adaptation involves adjustment in natural or human systems in response to actual or expected climatic stimuli or their effects, moderating harm or exploiting beneficial opportunities.

source_title: Climate Risk Management in Agricultural Extension for Ethiopia, 2nd Edition (CGIAR)
excerpt_text: Climate conditions impact crop and livestock production through a range of mechanisms. Solar radiation drives the conversion of atmospheric CO2 into plant biomass through photosynthesis. Temperature controls the rate of plant phenological development and most plant physiological processes. Precipitation determines the water available to plants from the soil and influences the availability and movement of soil nutrients. Potential evapotranspiration drives plants' uptake of water and nutrients from the soil. Temperature, humidity, and wind influence the population dynamics and movement of pests and pathogens. Climate impacts on livestock production tend to be more indirect. Severe or prolonged drought leads to widespread livestock mortality in pastoralism and other extensive livestock production systems in semi-arid to arid lands, by reducing rangeland, forage, and fodder plant productivity. Heat stress, from a combination of high temperatures and low potential evaporation, suppresses meat and milk production. Hydrometeorological hazards such as flooding, wind storms, and lightning can kill unprotected animals. Variations in the amount, timing, and distribution of precipitation are often the dominant source of year-to-year variability of production, income, and consumption in dryland agricultural systems in the tropics and in flood-prone locations. Biological response to climate conditions is generally nonlinear: for example, two regions with the same mean growing-season rainfall can have different mean yields, and higher rainfall variability results in lower mean yield.

source_title: Climate Risk Management in Agricultural Extension for Ethiopia, 2nd Edition (CGIAR)
excerpt_text: Timing is very important for agricultural management. Seasonality refers to the times of the year when agricultural activities occur and key reoccurring management decisions are made. Rainfed annual crop farmers make important decisions about land allocation and choice of crops and production inputs just before the start of the rainfall season. Decision time horizon refers to how far into the future a decision maker looks when evaluating the consequences of a decision option. The choice of what annual crop or cultivar to plant typically has a time horizon of 3 to 4 months, because productivity and profitability can be affected by conditions between planting and harvest. Decisions about field operations such as pest management, supplemental irrigation, or when to harvest have much shorter time horizons. On the other hand, the decision to plant or remove perennial crops such as coffee can have a planning horizon on the order of 5 to 10 years. Lead time refers to the time needed between making a decision and implementing the decision; some farm decisions require a period to prepare, for example to secure credit, purchase inputs, or contract labour or draught animals. For climate information to be useful for agricultural decision making, the time scale of the information should match the time horizon plus the lead time of the decision.

source_title: Climate Risk Management in Agricultural Extension for Ethiopia, 2nd Edition (CGIAR)
excerpt_text: There are important differences between the sequence of impacts of slow onset shocks such as drought and rapid onset shocks such as flooding and storms. A slow onset shock typically triggers a cascade of impacts: reduced crop production, increased staple food prices, reduced terms of trade for labour and capital goods, declining incomes, and reduced food consumption. Extreme weather events such as droughts, flooding, or high or low temperature extremes can lead to reduced food consumption and resulting health impacts. While a shock might impact an entire community, the severity of food security and health impacts differs among individuals due to differences in characteristics such as gender, age, asset ownership, and social capital. The adverse impacts of climate risk on food security can persist long after a period of climatic stress, a phenomenon known as a poverty trap.

source_title: Climate Risk Management in Agricultural Extension for Ethiopia, 2nd Edition (CGIAR)
excerpt_text: Conservation agriculture aims to sustainably improve and stabilize production through a combination of reducing soil disturbance from tillage, maintaining soil cover with organic material, and crop diversification through intercropping or rotations. Conservation agriculture is not a fixed technology but a varying bundle of practices that sometimes include additional soil fertility, water, or weed management practices. The yield and risk reduction benefits of conservation agriculture are associated with a combination of improved water infiltration and retention, accumulation of soil carbon, and reduced heat stress due to the presence of organic residues. Where these benefits have been observed, they generally increase over time and may not be realized in the first few years. Some studies have concluded that conservation agriculture shows greater risk management and productivity benefits in more drought-prone environments. The complexity of conservation agriculture, competing demand for organic residues, and the time lag before yield benefits are experienced have contributed to highly variable adoption rates and cases of dis-adoption in sub-Saharan Africa.

source_title: Climate Risk Management in Agricultural Extension for Ethiopia, 2nd Edition (CGIAR)
excerpt_text: Irrigation has the potential to dramatically increase productivity and reduce the risks associated with rainfed agriculture in dryland environments. The storage capacity of an irrigation system largely determines its capacity to buffer the agricultural impacts of climate variability. Large reservoir-based irrigation systems that can store enough water to meet demand for multiple agricultural seasons can protect crops from major droughts, but they are expensive to build, operate, and maintain, and often serve multiple water demands such as industrial, municipal, and hydroelectric power generation. Small-scale agricultural water management alternatives have lower capacity to buffer the impacts of prolonged or severe droughts but are generally more accessible to small-scale farmers due to their lower initial cost. Small-scale options include on-farm water harvesting and groundwater irrigation. Groundwater irrigation using electric, gasoline, or diesel pumps is often an option where the water table is sufficiently high and reliable. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture and the diminishing cost of solar panels have resulted in increasing attention to solar-powered groundwater irrigation. Rainwater harvesting is an alternative where groundwater irrigation is infeasible or impractical.

source_title: Climate Risk Management in Agricultural Extension for Ethiopia, 2nd Edition (CGIAR)
excerpt_text: Diversification is a well-known strategy for managing risk in fields as diverse as financial investments and agricultural production. Farmers can often use diversification to reduce their income and consumption risk, even if resource constraints limit their access to other risk management options. Farmers and agropastoralists have a range of options for diversifying their livelihoods, including farm and non-farm income sources, livestock species and breeds, crop species and cultivars, field locations and topography, and timing of production and marketing activities. Increasing the number of crop species does little to mitigate climate risk if all of the crops respond similarly to climate stresses, because their yields and returns are likely to be strongly correlated. Correlations of yields among crops or cultivars can be reduced if the timing of sensitivity to climatic stresses differs due to differing phenology or planting dates. Livestock are often treated as a form of savings and slaughtered or sold at strategic times, so the flexibility to use livestock as a buffer during periods of stress can make diversification between crop- and animal-based enterprises an effective risk management strategy. In an Africa-wide study using data from 28,000 households in 18 countries, households with more diversified production systems were generally better able to meet their consumption needs. The greatest opportunities for diversification of food crops, cash crops, and livestock are located in areas where annual rainfall has a mean in the range of 500 to 1000 mm and a coefficient of variability of annual rainfall in the range of 17 to 22 percent.

source_title: Yam (Dioscorea) Husbandry: Cultivating Yams in the Field or Greenhouse (Mignouna, Abang, Asiedu, Geeta, Cold Spring Harbor Protocols 2009)
excerpt_text: Yam (Dioscorea) is a tropical food crop grown in warm, sunny climates with temperatures between 25 and 30 degrees Celsius. Short days of 10-11 hours result in tuber formation, while days longer than 12 hours favor vine growth. Yams require deep, loose, well-textured loamy soil that is rich in organic matter and they do not tolerate waterlogged conditions. Yams are best planted at the beginning of the rainy season. Land should be cleared of bush and large tree stumps, with the debris allowed to decay and worked into the soil, then ploughed, harrowed and ridged or formed into mounds with hoes; the size of the mounds depends on the size of tubers desired at harvest. Yam seed tubers can also be planted on flat ground.

source_title: Yam (Dioscorea) Husbandry: Cultivating Yams in the Field or Greenhouse (Mignouna, Abang, Asiedu, Geeta, Cold Spring Harbor Protocols 2009)
excerpt_text: Large yam tubers can be cut into sets of 30 to 300 g depending on the desired tuber sizes at harvest, or planted as whole seed tubers. Before planting, treat the sets with a fungicide such as thiabendazole and allow them to air dry under shade (for example for 4 hours). Plant yam sets 10 cm deep in the soil to avoid exposure to the sun. Spacing depends on set size: the normally recommended spacing for commercial yam production is 1 m x 1 m between rows and stands (about 10,000 stands per hectare); use narrower spacing of 1 m x 0.25 m for smaller sets (for example 30 g). After planting, mulch the yam mounds and ridges. Water yam plants regularly during the growth cycle, particularly during the first 2-4 months of establishment.

source_title: Yam (Dioscorea) Husbandry: Cultivating Yams in the Field or Greenhouse (Mignouna, Abang, Asiedu, Geeta, Cold Spring Harbor Protocols 2009)
excerpt_text: Mulch around planted yam sets protects them from excessive heat and desiccation, especially in areas with hot temperatures and dry weather; it also adds organic matter to the soil, prevents soil erosion, preserves soil water, and increases microbial activity in the soil. Good mulching materials include dry grasses without seeds, broad leaves, compost manure, and cover crops. It is important to stake yam plants with bamboo sticks, branches from tree pruning, or PVC pipes 1-3 m high, either individually or in groups of two or three, or to construct a trellis for the vines; staking gives full exposure of leaves to light for photosynthesis and reduces disease. Guide and train the vines, particularly the lateral branches, to the stakes during active growth. Control weeds using manual hoeing, hand pulling, or herbicides, especially during the first 2-3 months after planting. If ridges or mounds diminish from rain splash or weeding, remold them to avoid exposing the growing tubers.

source_title: Yam (Dioscorea) Husbandry: Cultivating Yams in the Field or Greenhouse (Mignouna, Abang, Asiedu, Geeta, Cold Spring Harbor Protocols 2009)
excerpt_text: Fertilizer is optional for yam and should only be applied if necessary after a soil analysis. Split the fertilizer application to minimize leaching: first apply fertilizer about 1 month after emergence in a continuous band along the row of plants, about 10 cm away from the plants; then re-fertilize about 7-9 weeks later, when tuber bulking is in progress. Yams are harvested 7-8 months after planting, any time after large-scale leaf yellowing (senescence of the shoot) occurs in the field, though the exact timing depends on the variety. To harvest, dig around the tuber to loosen it from the soil, lift it, and cut it from the vine, avoiding bruising the tubers.

source_title: Yam (Dioscorea) Husbandry: Cultivating Yams in the Field or Greenhouse (Mignouna, Abang, Asiedu, Geeta, Cold Spring Harbor Protocols 2009)
excerpt_text: After harvest, sort yam tubers and grade them according to size and health status. Only healthy tubers that are free from nematodes, rots, cuts, insects, scrapes, and bruises can be stored. Cure freshly harvested tubers by stacking them and covering them with a canvas tarpaulin, exposing them for 5-7 days to a controlled temperature range of about 29-35 degrees Celsius and 90-95% relative humidity; during curing the skin thickens and new tissue forms under the surface of injured areas in the tuber. Store the yams in the shade with good ventilation and security from pests, for example in a barn on a raised platform. If tubers produce sprouts in storage and are not required for planting soon, detach the sprouts to avoid loss of tuber quality.

source_title: Yam (Dioscorea) Husbandry: Cultivating Yams in the Field or Greenhouse (Mignouna, Abang, Asiedu, Geeta, Cold Spring Harbor Protocols 2009)
excerpt_text: To minimize losses at harvest, dig around each yam tuber to loosen it from the soil, lift it, and cut it from the vine, and avoid bruising the tubers because damaged tubers cannot be stored well. Then sort the tubers and grade them according to size and health status; only healthy tubers free from nematodes, rots, cuts, insects, scrapes, and bruises may be kept for storage. Curing fresh tubers for 5-7 days at about 29-35 degrees Celsius and 90-95% relative humidity, for example stacked under a canvas tarpaulin, thickens the skin and heals injured areas. Store cured yams in a shaded, well-ventilated barn on a raised platform where pests cannot reach them, and detach any sprouts that appear in storage if the tubers are not needed for planting.

source_title: Millet and Sorghum Technology Toolkit Catalogue (TAAT/ICRISAT Clearinghouse, June 2022)
excerpt_text: Warrantage is a warehouse receipt system that provides inventory credit for stored grain, adapted to rural areas and smallholder families. It is limited to non-perishable produce such as millet, sorghum, and other grains whose prices rise in the months following harvest. Farmer organizations deposit their grain in a secured warehouse and obtain loans against the stored commodity. The warehouse is closed with two padlocks: the key for one lock is kept by the inventory credit committee secretary of the farmer organization, and the key for the other lock is kept by the financing body. The quality and weight of the grain and its packaging are registered by the inventory credit committee, and new sacks must be used to protect against pests. About five months after depositing produce, farmers must settle their loans before withdrawing sacks from the warehouse. Farmers benefit from the price difference between harvest time, when produce is abundant, and the dry season, when supply is short and prices are higher. Farmers who cannot store their grain are forced to sell at peak production times for low prices and often fall into debt because commercial loans demand collateral and carry high interest rates.

source_title: Millet and Sorghum Technology Toolkit Catalogue (TAAT/ICRISAT Clearinghouse, June 2022)
excerpt_text: Grain for warrantage storage must be properly prepared: separate chaff and stones, and dry it to about 10% moisture so warehouse space is used optimally and quality standards are met. Woven polypropylene 90-kg bags cost between US $0.25 and $0.50 each, while hermetic bags with a high-density plastic inner liner that prevent mold formation and insect attacks cost US $1 to $2 per 90-kg bag. Hiring guards to secure a warrantage warehouse usually costs US $75 to $150 per month. Sacks attacked by pests are set aside and the contents must be treated before return. Warrantage has been taken up by more than 350,000 farmers in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger; farmers there saw their income grow by 52% to 134%, and profits allowed them to purchase better seeds and fertilizers, increasing crop yields by 44% to 120%. Surveys in Burkina Faso reported that 60% of warehouse members were women. The system extends the food sufficiency period of rural communities from six to more than ten months.

source_title: Millet and Sorghum Technology Toolkit Catalogue (TAAT/ICRISAT Clearinghouse, June 2022)
excerpt_text: The mobile stover chopper/crusher processes crop residues such as sorghum and millet stalks into animal feed. A self-contained chopping and crushing machine costs US $1,250 to $1,700 depending on size, manufacturer, and country of origin; imported models are more expensive than locally fabricated ones. Machines usually come with a one-year guarantee and have a lifespan of about 10 years if well maintained. In the dryland belt of northern Nigeria, whole sorghum stalk costs between US $100 and $170 per ton on animal feed markets depending on quality, while one ton of crushed sorghum stover sells for US $330 to $500. Fuel consumption ranges from 2.5 to 3.5 liters per ton of stover. Processing stover offers an attractive business opportunity because value is added and market demand exists; machines provided to farmer associations in Niger produced and sold more than 100 tons of stover worth US $22,000 in less than six months. The main operating expenses are labor to collect material, carry it to the processing site, operate the machine, and load bags.

source_title: Millet and Sorghum Technology Toolkit Catalogue (TAAT/ICRISAT Clearinghouse, June 2022)
excerpt_text: Millet and sorghum flour are gluten-free and suitable for bread, biscuits, cakes, porridges, and even pasta. Sorghum flour has a mild, sweet flavor and smooth texture and can be used as a 1:1 all-purpose flour substitute; sorghum and wheat flour blends are well suited to yeast-leavened bread, flatbreads, cakes, muffins, cookies, and flour tortillas. Millet flour is used in the same way and as a 1:1 substitute for wheat flour, particularly in pancakes, flatbreads, muffins, and cakes, and makes a good thickener for stews. Whole millet and sorghum have long cooking times that are considerably reduced by processing into flour, offering savings on cooking time and fuel cost. Pearl millet's average composition is 70% carbohydrates, 16% protein, 5% fat, and 3% ash, and it is higher in phosphorus, iron, and calcium than maize or wheat. Sorghum typically contains 63% carbohydrate, 11% protein, 3% fat, and 2% ash, with varieties containing lower amounts of tannin most suitable for flour production.

source_title: Millet and Sorghum Technology Toolkit Catalogue (TAAT/ICRISAT Clearinghouse, June 2022)
excerpt_text: Before establishing a flour milling enterprise, market research is needed to identify a viable business model, including location, grain supply, and market, plus a full analysis of investment needs for capital equipment and labor. In general, 60% of the capital investment for a processing plant goes into equipment and the rest into construction and marketing. A small flour mill manually refilled with an output of 300-500 kg of flour per hour costs around US $3,500, while a fully automatic flour mill with a capacity of 30 tons per day costs about US $38,000. Modern milling equipment recovers 80-82% of flour from grain (and 18-20% bran), whereas traditional manual techniques recover only 65-70% flour; running at higher efficiency provides about US $30 additional net profit per ton of flour, and a 1% reduction in non-millable material adds about US $3 per ton of flour. Flour mills require skilled labor, regular inspections by a professional technician, and a reliable supply of electricity, with backup systems in place.

source_title: Rice Production Manual (TARI, Tanzania) - Modules 7-9: Salt-affected soils and rice productivity
excerpt_text: Salt-affected soils are categorized into three types: saline, sodic, and saline-sodic. Saline soils are dominated by calcium and magnesium cations, have electrical conductivity (EC) greater than 4 dS/m, sodium adsorption ratio (SAR) less than 13, and/or exchangeable sodium percentage (ESP) less than 15; they commonly show visible salt deposits on the surface and are called white alkali soils.
