Sodic soils have sodium ions dominating over calcium and magnesium, with EC less than 4 dS/m, SAR greater than 13, and/or ESP greater than 15, and pH generally higher than 8.5; the dispersion of soil particles destroys soil structure, prevents water movement by clogging pore spaces, and the soils often have a black color with a greasy surface, giving them the name black alkali or slick spots. Saline-sodic soils are high in both sodium and other salts, with EC greater than 4 dS/m, SAR greater than 13, and/or ESP greater than 15, and generally keep good soil structure; each type requires different management to become productive.

source_title: Rice Production Manual (TARI, Tanzania) - Modules 7-9: Salt-affected soils and rice productivity
excerpt_text: Salt in the root zone reduces crop yield by making it difficult for roots to extract water from the soil: salts increase the soil's osmotic potential, causing water to move from the plant tissue, where salt concentration is lower, into the soil where salt concentration is higher, so plants can wilt even when soil moisture is adequate. Salt also causes toxicity from excessive uptake of sodium, and reduces uptake of essential nutrients, particularly potassium and micronutrients. Extremely high salt stress kills the plant, while moderate to low salt stress reduces the rate of plant growth. The major symptoms of salt-affected soils on rice plants are: poor germination, poor root growth, patchy growth in the field, low tillering, stunted stems with shorter internodes, staggered non-uniform flowering, leaf rolling, white leaf blotches, leaf tips dying and burning from the tip, spikelet sterility, few spikelets per panicle, and light weight of grains.

source_title: Rice Production Manual (TARI, Tanzania) - Modules 7-9: Salt-affected soils and rice productivity
excerpt_text: Salt usually builds up in rice soils as a consequence of excessive use of irrigation water, especially in heavy soils with inadequate drainage, or the use of poor-quality salty irrigation water; farmers can also cause salt accumulation from injudicious use of fertilizers and other agro-inputs. Salts may also originate naturally from salt-bearing rocks at shallow depths: percolating rain or irrigation water dissolves the salts and brings them into the root zone when the water table rises, leaving them behind when the water evaporates. The best strategy to manage salt-affected soils is an integrated approach combining: an environment-modifying approach (leaching the root zone with clean water with low salt levels, providing good drainage, breaking the clay or silt layer, removing the surface layer, applying gypsum to replace sodium with calcium, and applying fertilizers), a crop-based approach (growing salt-tolerant crop varieties), and a hybrid approach combining both. The integrated approach is best because in most cases all types of salt-affected soils exist at different levels in one particular field.

source_title: Rice Production Manual (TARI, Tanzania) - Modules 7-9: Salt-affected soils and rice productivity
excerpt_text: Gypsum is used to displace sodium ions from soil colloids, and then large quantities of water are applied to wash and leach a substantial amount of the salts out of the root zone. Gypsum should be evenly broadcast and worked into a properly prepared, well-leveled field with bunds to retain water, 3-4 weeks prior to planting. Adequate water is then allowed into the field and the soil is stirred to help dislodge sodium ions and replace them with calcium; the field is left flooded for not less than 2 weeks, then the flood water is drained out, and this washing and draining exercise can be done 3-4 times. Gypsum provides calcium ions that flocculate the soil, making it more porous, and is also a good source of sulfur. Before transplanting, matured farmyard manure and basal fertilizers such as DAP and MOP are broadcast and worked into the washed field, and seedlings of salt-tolerant varieties such as SATO1 are transplanted at suitable spacing. A combination of gypsum and farmyard manure is more effective than either alone.

source_title: Rice Production Manual (TARI, Tanzania) - Modules 7-9: Salt-affected soils and rice productivity
excerpt_text: Farmyard manure helps manage salt-affected soils because when it decays it releases chemicals that break down sodium salts and make them more soluble, releases humic substances that improve soil structure by increasing flocculation, replenishes essential plant nutrients lost when the soil is drained, and feeds soil microbes that mineralize organic residues and fix atmospheric nitrogen. The actual rate of gypsum and farmyard manure is best determined after analysis of the salt-affected soil. Salt-tolerant rice varieties flourish better than other varieties in comparatively higher salt levels, so the cost of ameliorating the soil is reduced because smaller amounts of salts need to be removed. The salt-tolerant variety SATO1 (released 2016) has a potential yield of 6.0-8.5 tons per hectare and 4.5-5.0 tons per hectare under farmers' management, and still yields 2.0-4.0 tons per hectare under salt levels of ECe 5-7 dS/m and SAR 15-23; by comparison TXD306 (released 2001) yields 0.6-3.0 tons per hectare and Komboka (released 2012) yields 0.3-2.5 tons per hectare under the same salt levels.

source_title: Rice Production Manual (TARI, Tanzania) - Modules 7-9: Salt-affected soils and rice productivity
excerpt_text: Calcareous soils are affected by calcium-based salts and contain more than 15% calcium carbonate (CaCO3) in the soil, which can occur as powder, nodules, or crusts; heavily affected soil can have more than 50% CaCO3, making it powdery or pebble-like. They have high pH values of 7.5-8.5 which prevent or reduce the availability of many plant nutrients including nitrogen, phosphorus, magnesium, potassium, manganese, zinc, copper, and iron, and they generally have low organic matter content, so plants either produce very low yields or die. The best management approach is to use acid-forming materials to lower the soil pH and improve nutrient availability. A combination of sulfate of ammonia (SA) and diammonium phosphate (DAP) is used with farmyard manure: SA is top-dressed in 2 or more splits and is preferred to urea because it supplies nitrogen and sulfur and is the most acid-forming nitrogenous fertilizer, while DAP supplies the phosphorus usually lacking in calcareous soils and also lowers soil pH; farmyard manure also releases acids that reduce soil pH and replenishes nutrients.

source_title: Production Guide for Tomatoes (National Horticultural Research Institute, NIHORT Nigeria)
excerpt_text: Tomato (Lycopersicon esculentum) is an herbaceous plant of the Solanaceae family with a growth habit ranging from determinate to indeterminate types. Improved tomato varieties in Nigeria include: NHLe158-3, an indeterminate variety with big red fruits suitable for both South and North zones; Ife No 1, a determinate variety with round red fruits also suitable for both zones; Ibadan Local, an indeterminate variety with big pink fruits well adapted to the humid rainforest zone; NHLy11, a small to medium fruit (about 30 g) with firm flesh and good keeping quality, suitable for backyard gardens; and Roma VF, a determinate variety with pear-shaped red fruits suitable for planting in the North during the dry season. Tomato requires a cool dry climate for optimum production with a temperature range of 21-25 degrees Celsius, and a temperature of 15-21 degrees Celsius during fruit formation increases yields. It performs best on sandy loam to loamy soil with a pH of 6.0-6.5.

source_title: Production Guide for Tomatoes (National Horticultural Research Institute, NIHORT Nigeria)
excerpt_text: Tomato seed beds are usually prepared 50 cm wide and to any convenient length. Cover the seed beds with palm fronds to prevent the scorching effect of the sun, and pulverize and mix the soil with well decomposed animal manure or plant residues. Sterilize the soil by burning rice hull or rice straw on top of the seed bed for close to 5 hours to reduce damping off disease and insect pest damage; where this is not possible, an insecticide can be drenched into the soil at the recommended dosage. Sow tomato seeds in rows on the seed bed at a spacing of 5 cm apart and cover thinly with fine soil, then cover with palm fronds or elephant grass to reduce evaporation. Water the beds early in the morning and late in the evening or when necessary. Seeds germinate 3-5 days after sowing depending on soil temperature. Harden the seedlings one week before transplanting by gradually removing the shade, and the seedlings are ready for transplanting 4 to 5 weeks after sowing.

source_title: Production Guide for Tomatoes (National Horticultural Research Institute, NIHORT Nigeria)
excerpt_text: Land for tomato should be cleared at least four weeks before planting, especially virgin land, with stumping, ploughing, and harrowing; planting can be done at two-week intervals to allow weed seeds to germinate between operations. Tomatoes are transplanted when the seedlings are about 4-5 weeks old or about 10 cm tall, arranged on prepared beds 50 cm within rows and 75 cm between rows, giving a plant population of 26,667 plants per hectare. Organic fertilizer should be applied two weeks before transplanting, while NPK 15:15:15 compound fertilizer can be applied at the rate of 200-250 kg per hectare in two equal doses using the ring method: the first dose at about 3 weeks after transplanting and the second dose at fruit set. Stake tomatoes when sowing in the rainy season.

source_title: Production Guide for Tomatoes (National Horticultural Research Institute, NIHORT Nigeria)
excerpt_text: Tomato seedlings are staked at the peak of the rainy season using canes at least 1 m high, preferably bamboo. Staking advantages include exposing the fruit to light and air circulation, reducing the alternate heating and cooling of fruit by the soil which enhances fruit damage, reducing the incidence of diseases and pests, and providing good quality clean fruits. For weed control, the soil should be kept weed free from planting to early fruit set because weeds serve as alternate hosts of plant diseases and parasitize the root systems, affecting yield quantity and quality. Weed two or more times before harvesting is completed, with weeding 3-5 weeks after transplanting being desirable; increasing plant density also helps control weeds by casting shade on the undergrowth. Alternatively, apply Metribuzin herbicide at the rate of 1.0-1.5 kg active ingredient per hectare two days before transplanting for effective weed control.

source_title: Production Guide for Tomatoes (National Horticultural Research Institute, NIHORT Nigeria)
excerpt_text: For insect pest control in tomato, spray with 5 ml of Cypermetrin in 10 litres of water every week. Spray Dithane M45 at 20 g per 10 litres of water to control nematodes. The method of application depends on the type and mechanism of action of the pesticide, and can be through a motorized sprayer, a knapsack sprayer, or spot treatment. The complexity of pests and diseases in the environment often determines the frequency of pesticide application. Tomato seeds can be obtained from research centres such as NIHORT, government agencies such as the Ministry of Agriculture and ADPs, private seed companies, and farmer's plots or local markets.

source_title: Production Guide for Tomatoes (National Horticultural Research Institute, NIHORT Nigeria)
excerpt_text: Tomato fruits are ready for harvesting 12-18 weeks after sowing. Fruits are recommended for harvesting when half ripe or with a tint of colour change to ensure firmness and prevent damage during transportation; tomato fruits for processing must however be fully ripe before harvesting. Harvest at least once a week. Under good crop management, the tomato crop can be on the field for 17-23 weeks before harvesting is terminated. Yields of between 20-40 tons per hectare are obtainable under intensive cultivation, but yield depends on the agro-ecological zone: yield in the northern part of Nigeria can be up to 20 tonnes per hectare, and during the dry season irrigation facilities may be required to increase yield. Tomato production is profitable: based on the cost profile, every naira invested in tomato production is expected to yield 2.93 naira within 4 months.

source_title: Better groundnut through good agricultural practices (N2Africa, for farmers in Zimbabwe, 2014)
excerpt_text: Groundnut is a legume whose grains are very nutritious, containing much protein (23-25%) and oil (45-52%). The grains can be used directly for food or processed for cooking oil and other products, and have good market demand. The crop residues are rich in protein and are good feed for livestock or form a good basis for compost manure. Together with soil bacteria called rhizobia, groundnut forms root nodules that fix nitrogen from the air into a form the plant can use, which is why groundnut grows and yields very well in soils poor in nitrogen. Part of the fixed nitrogen is used to make protein in the grain, but some is left behind in the field and improves soil fertility, making groundnut a good crop to grow as an intercrop or in rotation with other crops. With good practices and the right varieties, grain yields can be as high as 4000 kg per hectare.

source_title: Better groundnut through good agricultural practices (N2Africa, for farmers in Zimbabwe, 2014)
excerpt_text: All soils other than very heavy soils are suitable for groundnut production, but groundnut grows best in sandy loam soil; it does not grow well and is difficult to harvest on very clayey soils. The soil pH should be between 5.3 and 7.3, and if the soil is acidic you can incorporate lime into the soil during land preparation to increase the pH. After growing groundnuts, grow other crops for at least 2 seasons before growing groundnut again on the same field to reduce the chance of diseases, pests, and weed problems. Avoid growing other legumes, tobacco, and tomatoes in rotation with groundnut, because this may cause build-up of nematodes. Well-prepared land ensures good germination and reduces weed infestation; the field can be prepared manually with a hoe, or with animal power or a tractor. In wet, low-lying areas, groundnut can be planted on ridges to prevent waterlogging, since waterlogging damages groundnut plants.

source_title: Better groundnut through good agricultural practices (N2Africa, for farmers in Zimbabwe, 2014)
excerpt_text: Select a good groundnut variety which suits your agro-ecological zone, paying attention to maturity period, growth habit, seed size, and oil content, and keep in mind that groundnut buyers may prefer a certain variety. The variety Natal Common has cream, small-sized grains, an attainable grain yield of about 4000 kg per hectare, a maturity period of about 120 days, a bunch growth habit, and poor pest and disease resistance; its seed rate is 80-100 kg per hectare. Other varieties include Nyanda (cream, large-sized grains) and Ilanda. Use only high quality seed for planting; do not plant damaged, small, or shrivelled seeds. Shell pods 1-2 weeks before sowing. To control seedling blights caused by soil bacteria and fungi, treat the seeds with fungicide: Thiram can be applied as a dust at 120 g per 100 kg of seed and mixed uniformly. Do a germination test at least 10 days before planting: plant 50 seeds; if at least 40 emerge the seed is good for planting, if 30-40 emerge plant more seeds than recommended, and get new seeds if less than 30 emerge.

source_title: Better groundnut through good agricultural practices (N2Africa, for farmers in Zimbabwe, 2014)
excerpt_text: Groundnut can fix nitrogen from the air, so it does not need nitrogen fertilizers such as ammonium nitrate or urea; it needs other nutrients such as phosphorus and calcium. Good phosphorus fertilizers are SSP and Compound L (which has high phosphorus content in relation to nitrogen). Place fertilizer in the furrow made for planting or in the planting hole, cover with 2-5 cm of soil, and place the seed on top. In sandy soils groundnut often fails to fill its pods and makes pops (empty pods); calcium ensures good pod filling, and gypsum is a good source of calcium. Apply gypsum to the soil just before flowering at a rate of 200-400 kg per hectare, and do not incorporate the gypsum into the soil to avoid damaging developing pods. SSP is applied at 225 kg per hectare and Compound L at 150 kg per hectare; when manure has been applied recently, rates can be reduced.

source_title: Better groundnut through good agricultural practices (N2Africa, for farmers in Zimbabwe, 2014)
excerpt_text: Plant groundnut when the soil is moist. Plant in rows which are 40-50 cm apart, and within rows plant seeds at 10 cm apart (1 seed per stand). Planting in rows has many advantages: you use the correct plant density, weeding is easier, and pods mature more uniformly, which makes it easier to decide when to harvest. If you apply fertilizer, first place the fertilizer in the planting furrow or hole and cover it with soil, then plant the seed. Plant seeds at a depth of 5 cm. Fill plant gaps one to two weeks after sowing, when plants have emerged.

source_title: Better groundnut through good agricultural practices (N2Africa, for farmers in Zimbabwe, 2014)
excerpt_text: Control weeds in groundnut to minimize competition for nutrients, water, sunlight, and space, either manually or chemically. Weed 2 or 3 times, with the first two weedings before flowering; earthing up (banking) can be done at the second weeding. Once flowering and pegging begins, weed by hand pulling instead of using a hoe, because hoe weeding might damage developing pods. Herbicides are available for pre-emergence or post-emergence weed control: Dual Magnum (Metalochlor, 1.1 l per ha), Sencor 480 SC (Metribuzin, 1.1 l per ha) and Lasso 48 EC (Alachlor, 2.5 l per ha) are pre-emergence herbicides, while Fusilade Super (Fluaziflop-p-butyl, 1.5 l per ha, for grasses) and Classic (Chlorimuron ethyl, 45 g per ha, for nutsedge and broad-leaved weeds) are post-emergence. If a pre-emergence herbicide is applied at planting, one weeding may be required at 5-6 weeks after planting. When in doubt, seek advice from an extension agent or agro-dealer.

source_title: Better groundnut through good agricultural practices (N2Africa, for farmers in Zimbabwe, 2014)
excerpt_text: Important groundnut pests include the groundnut leaf miner, the larvae of a small moth which burrows into the leaves; groundnut hopper (Hilda patreulis), a 5 mm long brown or green hopper that attacks the base of the stem below ground level and whose toxic saliva makes plants wither, turn yellow and die, with the first sign of infestation being black ants that feed on the honeydew excreted by the hoppers; termites, which can be controlled by removing residues of previous cereal crops and destroying termite mounds and removing queen termites, or by growing groundnut in fields with no previous termite history; and aphids, which transmit the rosette virus and can be controlled by spraying insecticides. To control the leaf miner, spray with the same insecticides as for aphids. Cutworms and leafhoppers can be controlled with Carbaryl at 1 kg per hectare, aphids with Dimethoate 40EC at 1 litre per hectare, and bollworms and cutworms with Karate (lambda-cyalothrin) at 0.14 litre per hectare. Birds, rats and squirrels feed on improperly buried seeds or dig up seeds: scare birds away and fence the field to control rodents.

source_title: Better groundnut through good agricultural practices (N2Africa, for farmers in Zimbabwe, 2014)
excerpt_text: Leaf spot is a fungal disease of groundnut. Early leaf spot can occur two weeks after crop emergence, showing roughly circular lesions with yellow (chlorotic) halos surrounding darker lesions and a lighter shade of brown on the lower surface of the leaves; late leaf spot occurs late in the season with almost round lesions darker than those of early leaf spot. Early leaf spot often reduces yield more than late leaf spot. Leaf spot pathogens survive mainly in crop debris, so crop rotation, burying crop debris during land preparation, and early planting help reduce the disease. Groundnut rosette is caused by viruses transmitted by aphids; infected plants show chlorotic (yellow and stunted) or green (green and stunted) symptoms, and late planting and wide spacing increase its incidence. Rosette can be controlled by planting a resistant variety or spraying insecticides to control the aphids that spread the disease. Grey mould is a fungal disease that infects at ground level with a light grey fungal rot, favoured by cool temperatures and wet conditions.

source_title: Better groundnut through good agricultural practices (N2Africa, for farmers in Zimbabwe, 2014)
excerpt_text: Aflatoxin is a toxic substance causing sickness, hepatitis and/or liver cancer, produced by fungi that can grow on groundnut, with contamination possible before and after harvest; pods should not be damaged in the field, and export groundnuts must have very low aflatoxin levels. Harvest at the right time: harvesting too early causes yield losses and too late encourages aflatoxin contamination. Groundnut is mature when the inside of the pods darken: dig up about five plants from different parts of the field, remove and open the pods, and if three quarters of the pods open easily and have dark markings inside, start harvesting. Preferably harvest during a dry period; dig up the plants and either remove the pods immediately or dry the plants in the sun for up to 2 weeks, then pull off the pods, removing soil from the pods before drying to prevent aflatoxin. Grade the pods and remove shrivelled, diseased, broken, and immature pods. Do not shell groundnuts if you want to store them. Store pods in clean bags; if re-using bags, wash and disinfect them by boiling in water for 5 minutes (do not let polyethylene bags touch the outside of the pot or they will melt). Clean the storage room, remove old grains and insects, do not store grain in the same place as pesticides, stack bags on a raised platform or wooden pallet away from the wall, avoid direct contact with the ground, and inspect regularly to remove infested or rotting grains.

source_title: Growing Pepper in Nigeria (Commercial Crop Production Guide Series)
excerpt_text: Peppers are used in stew and local dishes across Nigeria. The varieties commonly produced are: bird pepper (atawere, Capsicum frutescens); cayenne pepper or red pepper (sombo, Capsicum frutescens); atarodo (Capsicum annum); and tatase (Capsicum annum). The fruits vary in size, color, shape, and pungency. Bird pepper and cayenne pepper are both hot and are used either fresh or dried, while atarodo and tatase are mostly used fresh.

source_title: Growing Pepper in Nigeria (Commercial Crop Production Guide Series)
excerpt_text: Select a good soil medium for raising pepper seedlings: the soil should be rich, well-drained, and free of diseases and insect pests. A mixture of compost and topsoil in equal proportions can be used to make seed beds or fill trays (30 x 45 x 8 cm). Make beds about 1 metre long with a 1 metre path between beds, and keep the bed surface level to avoid erosion. In the absence of an appropriate soil mixture, apply 1 kg (or 3 small milk tins) of 15:15:15 compound fertilizer per bed of 10 square metres, or 2-4 head pans of well-rotted farmyard or poultry manure plus 1 milk tin of superphosphate and 2 milk tins of sulphate of ammonia. It is usual to treat nursery soil with fumigant to kill pests, fungi, and weeds: VAPAM is recommended at 1 litre to 20 litres of water per bed of 1 m x 10 m; wet the soil heavily to a depth of 15 cm, cover with palm fronds, and do not sow seeds until 9-10 days after treatment. In the absence of fumigants, apply heat treatment by burning trash on the beds and removing the ash.

source_title: Growing Pepper in Nigeria (Commercial Crop Production Guide Series)
excerpt_text: Water the pepper nursery well a day before sowing. Make drills about 5-10 cm apart across the bed and sow about 100 seeds per drill, then cover lightly. Thin the seedlings to 1 per 2.5 cm of drill 15-20 days after sowing. Alternatively, make holes 4 x 4 cm apart on the bed and drop 3-4 seeds in each hole, thinning later to one per hole. Provide shade in the nursery to protect seedlings from hot sun and heavy rains: a palm frond on a half-metre pole framework is adequate; remove half of the fronds 30 days after sowing and the rest 40 days later to harden the seedlings before transplanting. Water the seedlings every morning, reducing the quantity and frequency during hardening. Watering should be moderate: over-watering may make plants soft and susceptible to diseases such as damping off. The seedlings should be sprayed regularly with insecticides like Ambush and fungicide Dithane for control of insects and diseases before they are transplanted.

source_title: Growing Pepper in Nigeria (Commercial Crop Production Guide Series)
excerpt_text: Plough, harrow, and make beds a week before transplanting pepper. Make beds 1.0 metre wide and of any convenient length, arranging the plants in two rows on the bed: the rows are spaced 70 cm apart while the plants are spaced 50 cm apart within the rows. Water the seed trays and beds in the nursery before lifting the seedlings. A complete fertilizer such as NPK 15:15:15 can be applied about 2 weeks after transplanting at the rate of one matchbox of fertilizer to two plants: draw a circle round the base of the plant, carefully spread the fertilizer in the groove, and cover lightly with soil, keeping the circle a distance of about 4-7 cm from the stem. The second application should be performed at 50% flowering at a rate of one matchbox per plant, watering the plant immediately after applying the fertilizer.

source_title: Growing Pepper in Nigeria (Commercial Crop Production Guide Series)
excerpt_text: The most important pest of pepper is the fruit fly (Ceratitis capitata), which feeds on the fruit flesh leaving only the transparent skin. Borers (Lepidopterae spp.) are sometimes found in the fruits as well, and scales and mealybugs occur mainly on the stems of older plants. To control these pests, spray every week with either Sevin 85 WP at 10 g per 10 litres of water or other suitable insecticides.

source_title: Growing Pepper in Nigeria (Commercial Crop Production Guide Series)
excerpt_text: Bacterial wilt is a very serious disease of pepper: infected plants show wilting and death of the growing point and upper leaves. Control it by removing and destroying affected plants and using disease resistant varieties. Virus-infected pepper plants show reduction in size of young leaves with leaf curl, mottling, and vein clearing, puckering and curling inwards of leaves, and stunted growth with shorter internodes and a bunchy top; control viruses by practicing crop rotation, since pepper should not be grown on the same plot for 3 or 4 years. Fruit rot (Colletotrichum capsici) can cause considerable loss of fruits. Harvest pepper fruits when they are red or start to turn red, for example atarodo and tatase fruits, and harvest once or twice a week to allow enough time for ripening. With good care tatase and atarodo can remain productive for 2 years, while sombo and atawere are shorter-lived; fruit yield of 3-6 tonnes is expected.

source_title: Pepper Production Guide (Ghana Ministry of Food and Agriculture)
excerpt_text: Thrips (Thrips tabaci) damage pepper by feeding on young leaves, which turn narrow, twisted, or crumpled, fail to elongate, and finally may wilt and dry giving the plant a scorched appearance; thrips excreta are visible as small black dots on leaves, and thrips start infesting the plant before the flowers open, causing the flowers to die and become brown. Begin monitoring at flower bud initiation: pick and open flower buds to assess for larvae or adult thrips, or shake the flowers onto a piece of white paper. Spray with a Deltamethrin product at 75-100 ml per 15 litres of water or Lambda Cyhalothrin product at 35-40 ml per 15 litres of water. Remove alternative hosts such as Centrosema and Musa spp. from production fields and intercrop with maize or sorghum to reduce thrips populations. Mites are tiny and live on the underside of leaves, tender stems, fruits, flower peduncles, and flowers; damage shows as stippling of light dots on leaves that may take on a bronze color, and attacked fruits become deformed with a cork-like surface or fail to develop. Check the undersides of leaves for mites, eggs, and webbing with a hand lens, and spray with Sulphur 80 WP at 70 ml per 15 litres of water, neem extracts at 1 matchbox per litre of water, or pawpaw leaf extract at 12 large matured leaves per 16-litre knapsack at 80 litres per hectare at 10-day intervals during flowering. Adequate watering during drought also helps because mite damage is worse on drought-stressed plants.

source_title: Pepper Production Guide (Ghana Ministry of Food and Agriculture)
excerpt_text: Anthracnose (ripe fruit rot), caused by Colletotrichum spp., is a major problem of ripened pepper fruits and occurs when there is localized waterlogging within the farm, resulting in thick black spots that render fruits unmarketable; symptoms are circular dark sunken lesions with concentric rings on immature and mature fruit, and irregularly shaped brown spots with dark edges on stems and leaves. Prevention: use certified seeds or disease-free seedlings, soak seeds in hot water (50 degrees Celsius) for 30 minutes before planting, ensure good drainage, control weeds, and rotate pepper every 2 years with non-host crops such as maize, sorghum, or groundnuts. Control by applying Maneb at 30-45 g per 15 litres or Folpet at 45 g per 15 litres of water, and destroy diseased plants and fruits by burying or burning. Fusarium wilt is caused by a fungus that lives indefinitely in the soil and is spread in irrigation water; it is very susceptible to changes in temperature and soil moisture, develops optimally at 24-27 degrees Celsius, does not occur in dry soil, but is serious in poorly drained fields. Symptoms are yellowing and wilting of leaves and stems, often affecting one side of the plant, with internal dark brown discolouration of the stem. There are no effective chemicals for fusarium wilt: prevent it by avoiding land with a history of wilt, solarising the soil with plastic sheets 6-8 weeks before planting, rotating the nursery site each season, maintaining good drainage, planting tolerant local varieties such as Mesiwa, destroying plant debris by burning, practicing long rotation of 6 years with non-solanaceous plants after 3 seasons, disinfecting farm tools with 10% bleach solution, and avoiding sites with nematode damage.

source_title: Pepper Production Guide (Ghana Ministry of Food and Agriculture)
excerpt_text: Root-knot nematodes cause stunted growth and zones of poor growth in pepper fields soon after transplanting, with wilting and yellowing of plants; uproot affected plants and examine the root system for galls and swellings. Nematicides are generally poisonous and expensive and should generally not be recommended to smallholder farmers. Prevent nematodes by rotating for 2 years with non-host crops such as sorghum, millet, broccoli, or cauliflower, planting marigolds (Tagetes patula) on the fields for two months after harvest and ploughing them into the soil before transplanting, exposing ploughed land 2-3 weeks before transplanting, controlling weeds and volunteer solanaceous plants, washing soil particles off farm tools after use, and roguing and burning affected plants at early stages of growth. Applications of poultry manure or cow dung at 5 tonnes per hectare boost crop vigour and reduce nematode infestations. Damping off is a rot that occurs at soil level of young seedlings caused by fungi, showing dark shrivelled stems around the base and brown rotten roots, with wilting, collapse, and death of seedlings. Prevent it by sowing seeds thinly for aeration, planting in raised beds with good drainage, avoiding over-watering and excessive fertilization at the nursery, treating seed with Mancozeb 800 g/kg or Folpet 500 g/l at 3-4 g per kg of seed, solarising nursery soil with clear plastic, disinfecting tools with 10% bleach or fire, and removing infected plants as soon as symptoms appear.

source_title: Pepper Production Guide (Ghana Ministry of Food and Agriculture)
excerpt_text: Peppers are ready for harvesting 6-8 weeks after transplanting; harvest red ripe or green depending on market demand. The second harvesting is done after 10 to 14 days, and from then on harvest once every week, though the yield can drop after the 11th week. Depending on the condition of the pepper, harvesting can continue beyond 6 months if there is no disease outbreak. To harvest, snap the fruit stalk from the stem by hand. Plants kept for continued production must still be provided with nutrients, especially more potassium and less nitrogen. If the local market is the target, the peppers are left to ripen and could take 8-9 weeks before harvesting; they are then parboiled and dried before selling. Harvested peppers should be placed in the shade immediately after harvest and cooled as soon as possible. Pepper can be produced for both local and export markets, but producers should identify potential buyers who will give them an assurance of buying their pepper before commencing production activities, since market conditions vary.

source_title: Goat production and commercialization - paravet manual (CARE & ILRI, imGoats Project, 2013)
excerpt_text: A healthy goat walks well, is active, alert and has a lively look, eats and drinks well and ruminates after meals, has a smooth and shiny pelt, breathes normally, and has clear urine and droppings with normal consistency. A sick goat changes its behavior or appearance: it walks alone and is depressed, is aggressive or anxious, is weak with fallen head and tail, has diarrhea, lies down, has liquids running down from the nose or eyes or other openings, does not walk well or limps, does not eat normally (stops grazing or drinking water), is very slim, has a big swollen belly, breathes with difficulty, has wounds on the body, or has a high body temperature. When an animal is not well, separate it from the healthy animals immediately and call the paravet to assist, while still feeding and watering it. If a sick animal is not treated it can get worse and die, transmit the disease to other animals and cause major losses, never become a good breeder or a good animal for sale, or carry diseases transmissible to humans.

source_title: Goat production and commercialization - paravet manual (CARE & ILRI, imGoats Project, 2013)
excerpt_text: Goats get sick because of limited feeding, contact of healthy animals with sick animals, water or pasture contaminated with droppings, and parasites present in the pasture or in the shelters. Prevention is better than cure: feed the animals well as this makes them more resistant to diseases, always give them clean water to drink, keep the goat shelter clean and well ventilated, separate sick from healthy animals so disease is not transmitted, treat against internal and external parasites regularly (twice a year), and give goats vaccinations provided by the Veterinary Services where applicable. Some diseases can be treated with dewormers while others need drugs such as antibiotics; the best is to call a paravet to assess the situation and treat accordingly. After drug administration, animals should not be slaughtered and consumed immediately; ask the paravet how many days you should wait.

source_title: Goat production and commercialization - paravet manual (CARE & ILRI, imGoats Project, 2013)
excerpt_text: Parasites are very small animals that live by benefiting from other animals. Internal parasites live inside the animal's body, such as worms; external parasites live on the animal's skin, such as ticks, and can cause wounds and abscesses, and ticks can cause diseases that result in diarrhea. An animal with parasites is skinny, sad, gets sick easily, has difficulties reproducing, and can have wounds on the skin. Goats get parasites in the pasture area especially when there is overgrazing, in shelters that are not clean, and when they are near other goats with parasites. Ticks on the grass stick to the goat's hair when grazing, suck blood, and fall on the ground to lay eggs; worm eggs are swallowed with grass, develop in the intestines, and are expelled with droppings, contaminating more grass. To prevent and treat parasites, deworm goats twice each year (once at the end of the dry season or beginning of the rainy season, and again at the end of the rainy season or beginning of the dry season), deworm young goats after weaning, do not deworm pregnant goats during the first month of gestation to avoid harming the fetus, rotate the grazing areas, and build the goat shelter in an elevated and dry location and keep it clean. If the animal is seriously ill, apart from a dewormer it can be given an antibiotic to treat possible secondary infections.

source_title: Goat production and commercialization - paravet manual (CARE & ILRI, imGoats Project, 2013)
excerpt_text: A goat shelter protects animals from rain and adverse weather, provides shade, makes it easier to restrain animals when we need to treat or observe them, and helps protect the animals against thieves and predators. Whenever possible, build the shelter on an elevated and dry location. The floor should be above ground level (0.6 to 1 m) and made of bamboo or thin poles or stakes placed at approximately one finger distance from each other to allow droppings to fall on the ground, preventing the animals from being in contact with urine and droppings and hence parasites. The shelter should be covered to avoid rainwater entering, and open enough to allow sunlight to enter in the mornings and late afternoons so it stays dry and well ventilated. There should be supplemental feeding in the shelter in the dry season and clean water near the shelter always. The shelter should be at least 1.5 square metres for each doe with kid and 1 square metre for other animals. A dirty shelter is a source of diseases: clean the shelter at least once a week, collect the droppings underneath at least once a week and keep them separate, and after some weeks use them as manure for the cropping areas.

source_title: Goat production and commercialization - paravet manual (CARE & ILRI, imGoats Project, 2013)
excerpt_text: Just like people need a balanced diet, goats also need good feeding to grow healthy. It is very important for goats to have a diverse diet consisting of grass, shrubs, and tree leaves. Goat keepers can cut and give their goats crop residues (maize, sorghum, cassava, peanuts), vegetable leaves (cassava, sweet potato, pumpkin), vegetable leftovers, and native and planted vegetation such as leucaena, mulberry, and velvet bean. It is important for goats to eat leaves from trees and shrubs that give pods, because they are usually rich in minerals and vitamins important for the good development of the animals. Water goats daily with clean water free of droppings. In the rainy season animals are fatter because they have more feed available; in the dry season animals are thin because of reduced pasture. To mitigate feed scarcity during the dry season, preserve grass as hay bales in the rainy season, and give crop residues and leaves of forage trees to the animals in the dry season.

source_title: Goat production and commercialization - paravet manual (CARE & ILRI, imGoats Project, 2013)
excerpt_text: Overgrazing happens when animals stay for too long on the same pasture, eat all that exists, and deplete the pasture so it is not productive the following year; when the pasture is depleted, the animals start suffering and get skinny and sicker. For the pasture to continue growing it is necessary to have seeds in the earth, so it is important to move animals to different grazing sites regularly (rotation of grazing areas). Pasture rotation is a systematic way of moving the animals around over various pasture areas; it prevents overgrazing and even depletion of the area, and it helps to control parasites. Animals should graze freely and not be tethered; goats and cattle can graze on the same area because they will eat different plants. The pasture area should have varied vegetation, and young animals, being less resistant to diseases, should graze in cleaner sites with fewer parasites. It is dangerous to burn grazing areas: fires destroy many shrubs that goats can eat, uncontrolled fires can destroy pasture and endanger houses, people and animals, they leave the soil exposed to the sun and rains possibly causing erosion, and they can destroy important medicinal plants for the community.

source_title: Goat production and commercialization - paravet manual (CARE & ILRI, imGoats Project, 2013)
excerpt_text: Good reproductive management allows maintaining the same flock size while generating income by selling offspring, and good quality and quantity of offspring generates higher income through sales. One buck is enough to mate 20-30 does: if you have more than 30 does you will need more bucks. It is not worthwhile to have more breeder males than necessary, because they will start fighting for the does and get hurt, they can cause abortion in pregnant does, and a lot of bucks in a flock does not result in more pregnant does. Choose the does and buck with the best characteristics: the most sturdy and healthy, well built, without undesirable characteristics; bucks should have both testicles well descended and should not be from the same family as the does they are going to mate. Castration (with a burdizzo) of the bucks not needed for breeding has many advantages: castrated bucks put on weight faster than non-castrated bucks, are easier to sell, produce meat of better quality that does not smell and is tenderer, the number of abortions caused by mating attempts on pregnant does is reduced, they are quieter and fight less, and it avoids propagation of undesirable characteristics in the flock. Castrate animals as soon as possible, when the animal is young and before 3 months of age; old bucks that are not needed for reproduction could be castrated and sold afterwards.

source_title: Goat production and commercialization - paravet manual (CARE & ILRI, imGoats Project, 2013)
excerpt_text: Planning parturitions ensures kids are born at a time that is more advantageous: when you want to sell, when there is more pasture, and when you have less work in the field. The gestation period of goats is 5 months, so the mating time has to be 5 months before the desired time of parturition: for example, for kids to be born in February, the does must be mated in September, and the kids can then be sold at 10 months of age. Does approaching parturition get agitated and keep away from the flock, so they should be in a safe place where they can be assisted if necessary; it is safer for kids to be born in the shelter rather than in the pasture where they might be attacked by wild animals, and separating pregnant does from the flock prevents abortions due to harassment by other goats. Pregnant does should not walk for long distances, especially during the last months of gestation, and should be fed well and always have clean water. Kids should drink the first milk (colostrum) shortly after birth, as it has important ingredients that make them strong and able to resist diseases. The best time for a doe to mate for the first time depends on weight, not age: a doe that has reached three quarters of its adult weight is ready for mating; for example, if the normal weight of an adult doe is 20 kg, it can be mated at 15 kg. Only healthy does should be mated; a doe that gets pregnant when too young has to share energy between her own development and the kid, never fully develops, and her kids are often small and weak and can easily die. To increase reproductive performance, carefully choose breeding bucks and does, replace the breeding bucks every 2 to 4 years with younger and stronger animals from other villages so they will not be from the same family as the does, castrate males that are not good for reproduction, sell or slaughter does with undesirable characteristics, and keep the animals well fed and dewormed.

source_title: Goat production and commercialization - paravet manual (CARE & ILRI, imGoats Project, 2013)
excerpt_text: People keep goats as a way of saving money, for consumption, for selling, for offering, and to give prestige in the community. Not all money from selling animals is profit: you have to think of the costs of rearing the animal, such as deworming, treatments, transportation to the market, and the herder. Out of the money received from selling an animal (revenue) you have to put aside what you spent on that animal; the remaining amount is gain or profit: revenue minus costs equals profit (for example, selling a doe for 900 meticais while spending 60 on it, 40 on treatment and 20 to go to market, gives a profit of 780). When you sell animals, invest part of the money in the flock so the business can continue thriving: buy good quality animals for reproduction, deworm the animals, save money for when the animals need treatment, and buy construction materials for a goat shelter. If you do not invest in the flock, weak animals or those with undesirable characteristics may mate and produce weak offspring, you will have less offspring, some animals may get sick and die, and you may end up with no animals. To increase profit: keep the animals healthy (well fed, dewormed, with water to drink), treat diseases quickly, sell animals when they are young and healthy at around 8 to 10 months old (old animals cost more to keep healthy and are often sold at a lower price), and keep a balanced flock composition with many does and only one breeding buck per 30 does.

source_title: Make a Living through Fish Farming - tilapia (CTA Practical Guide Series No. 9)
excerpt_text: Fish farming is the best option for producing more fish in Eastern Africa because almost all natural fish stocks have been over-exploited while demand continues to increase. Fish grow quickly and give a return on investment fast: a tiny fingerling is ready to eat in as little as six to eight months, when it can fetch around US $0.70, about 25 times more than the cost price. You do not have to be next to an ocean, lake, river, or stream to farm fish, although a constant source of clean fresh water is essential for tilapia farming. There is a ready market both locally and internationally, and you can harvest only what you can sell to avoid wastage. Fish rarely suffer from diseases unlike other types of livestock, and land unsuited to other productive uses, even small plots, can be used for fish farming. Fish is very nutritious, providing high-quality protein and other essential nutrients which are especially important for mothers and growing children.

source_title: Make a Living through Fish Farming - tilapia (CTA Practical Guide Series No. 9)
excerpt_text: Rectangular ponds are easier to build and the fish are easier to catch compared to round ponds, and ponds should not be dug in the path of a river to avoid flooding and washing away of the fish. Apply a thin layer of agricultural lime to the bottom of the pond to help eliminate pests like leeches. Fill the pond with water so that the shallow end is 0.5 metres deep and the deep end is 1.5 metres deep, and keep the water levels between 0.5 and 1.5 metres deep. Keep the area around the pond clear of weeds, and fence the pond to keep out children and animals.

source_title: Make a Living through Fish Farming - tilapia (CTA Practical Guide Series No. 9)
excerpt_text: Pond fertilization encourages the growth of tiny plants called algae and tiny animals that provide food for the fish. Algae turn the water green, which makes it harder for predators such as birds and snakes to see and catch the fish. To fertilize the pond you may use animal manures or chemical fertilizers. For every 100 square metres of pond area use: 6 kg of cow, goat, or sheep dung; 2.5 kg of chicken, duck, or goose droppings; or 1 kg of chemical fertilizer such as Urea, DAP (diammonium phosphate), or TSP (triple superphosphate).

source_title: Make a Living through Fish Farming - tilapia (CTA Practical Guide Series No. 9)
excerpt_text: A fingerling seed is a tiny, newly hatched fish weighing between 20 and 80 grammes. Purchase tilapia fingerlings from an established fish farm within your area, place them in a bucket of fresh water, and move them to your fish pond as soon as possible, within 6 hours. Add three tilapia fingerlings for each square metre of pond area: a pond 10 metres by 10 metres has an area of 100 square metres and would need 300 fingerlings. To stock the pond, gently lower the bucket containing the fingerlings into the shallow end of the pond and gradually tip it to allow the fingerlings to swim into the pond; if fingerlings are not introduced gently they may die from shock.

source_title: Make a Living through Fish Farming - tilapia (CTA Practical Guide Series No. 9)
excerpt_text: For the first month, young tilapia fingerlings eat the natural food in the pond. After the first month, feed the fingerlings twice daily with suitable foods such as rice, maize, or wheat bran (a quarter of a kilogramme fed twice daily), sliced kale (sukuma wiki), chopped sweetpotato vines, termites and ants, small lake shrimps, small leftover fish caught by fishermen, or local fishmeal (omena, dagaa, or mukene dust). Check on the fish regularly and weigh them monthly to see how they are growing: catch some fish using a scoop net with some feed placed inside as bait. The fingerlings should have increased in weight by at least 10 grammes in the first month and continue to grow steadily each month.

source_title: Make a Living through Fish Farming - tilapia (CTA Practical Guide Series No. 9)
excerpt_text: Fish can be harvested partially, leaving at least ten fish in the pond to breed, or totally, harvesting all fish and cleaning the pond, six months after stocking. Lower the fishing net into the pond at the deep end, ideally with two people on either side of the pond holding the net, press the net to the bottom of the pond to ensure you catch all the fish (this can best be done by having three people in the pond), gradually pull the net towards the shallow end, gather the net to one corner making sure you retain all fish captured, and pull out the net. Place the fish in a container of clean water, sort them, return any underweight fish to the pond, and depending on demand, market all fish or return some to the pond.

source_title: Make a Living through Fish Farming - tilapia (CTA Practical Guide Series No. 9)
excerpt_text: After harvesting fish, immediately cut the fish open along the underside and pull out the guts; the guts can be dried, mixed with bran, and fed to livestock including chickens. Wash the fish with clean water and place them in cooler boxes, and sell or cook and eat fresh fish as soon as possible, otherwise preserve fish by salting, smoking, or sun drying. Keep simple records of costs and income from sales to work out whether the fish-farming business is profitable. Troubleshooting: for contaminated water, ensure the water is clean and safe before building the pond; for stunted growth of fish, feed regularly with recommended feeds; if fish are poisoned by Tephrosia bark, clear Tephrosia trees from the area around the pond and add more water to dilute the poison as soon as possible; to prevent loss of fish to snakes, monitor lizards, and fish-eating birds such as kingfishers and herons, clear the pond site and fertilize the pond to make the water green; to prevent theft, fence the pond and keep watch when fish mature; against leech damage, apply lime at the pond bottom before stocking; to avoid fish being washed away by floods, ensure the maximum water level does not exceed 1.5 metres; and during long dry spells with shortage of water supply, harvest the fish and sell before the drought.

source_title: Nigeria Guidebook on Regulatory Aspects of Dissemination of Public Varieties (NML/SFSA/AVISA, 2019)
excerpt_text: In Nigeria and throughout sub-Saharan Africa, the public sector is heavily involved in seed breeding, but regulatory processes at national and regional levels affect whether public seed varieties reach the market. Nigeria's seed system is governed by the 2019 National Agricultural Seeds Council (NASC) Act, which repealed the previous National Agricultural Seeds Act. Through the NASC Act, Nigeria has harmonized its legal and regulatory framework with the ECOWAS Seed Regulations, recognizing the West African Catalogue of Plant Species and Varieties (WACPSV). Under ECOWAS rules, a variety entered into the national catalogue of one Member State becomes part of the WACPSV, and once in the WACPSV a variety should be freely traded and allowed for multiplication throughout the ECOWAS region without any further registration requirements. The ECOWAS Seed Regulations cover eleven priority crops important for food security and trade: maize, pearl millet, rice, sorghum, cassava, Irish potato, yam, onion, tomato, cowpea, and groundnut.

source_title: Nigeria Guidebook on Regulatory Aspects of Dissemination of Public Varieties (NML/SFSA/AVISA, 2019)
excerpt_text: A new variety must be registered before it can be commercialized and sold in the Nigerian market. Variety registration follows a process of field testing: new domestic varieties must undergo on-station DUS (distinctness, uniformity, and stability) trials for at least one year, multi-location VCU (variety for cultivation and use) trials for two seasons across at least 10 testing sites per year in different agro-ecological zones, and on-farm trials for one year on at least 10 farmers' fields supervised by extension services. The process is reviewed by a Technical Sub-Committee on Crops and approved by the National Crop Varieties and Animal Breeds Registration and Release Committee (NVRC). According to the 2019 TASAI report, the entire variety release and registration process takes on average 43 months and costs between US $2,000 and $27,000, with costs varying by the proximity of breeders to different sites and the number of varieties being tested. If a variety is registered, 5 kg of breeder's seed is deposited in the National Genebank and 50 kg of foundation seed is given to NASC for certification. If the variety is registered under a regional system such as ECOWAS, testing may be waived entirely by the Minister of Agriculture on the advice of the Technical Sub-Committee on Crops.

source_title: Nigeria Guidebook on Regulatory Aspects of Dissemination of Public Varieties (NML/SFSA/AVISA, 2019)
excerpt_text: After a variety is released and registered, it must be certified before it can be sold in the Nigerian market, and the certification process is aligned with ECOWAS regulations and international standards. The NASC Act creates an Official Certification Service with the mandate to oversee seed certification and quality control, and NASC may authorize private certification bodies to undertake quality control and seed certification on its behalf and under its supervision, which is expected to fast-track the process and reduce NASC's workload. The NASC Act also creates a fund for NASC to cover all expenses involved in the administration of the Act. Specific regulations that establish the certification requirements and procedures have not yet been put in place, which creates some uncertainty in the seed sector. The World Bank Enabling the Business of Agriculture (EBA) 2019 estimated that registering a variety in Nigeria costs 171.6% of income per capita, roughly USD $3,569. Nigeria ranked 67th out of 101 EBA countries overall, with a supply-of-seed score of 49.17 out of 100.

source_title: Nigeria Guidebook on Regulatory Aspects of Dissemination of Public Varieties (NML/SFSA/AVISA, 2019)
excerpt_text: Licensing agreements are contracts between two parties in which one party authorizes another to use and commercialize a plant variety in exchange for a royalty payment; they have been used in Africa with positive outcomes. In Nigeria, licensing agreements can be used to transfer the right to commercialize an already registered variety to a private seed company, or to authorize a private company to register a variety in the national or regional catalogue on behalf of a public institution. In exchange for use rights, the private company agrees to pay a royalty fee to the public breeder, creating an alternative source of income for research institutions that can be reinvested in future variety development. Licensing agreements are not only possible under Plant Breeders' Rights (PBR); public institutions in many African countries have used them for varieties that are not protected under PVP frameworks. For example, the Kenya Agriculture and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) has used licensing agreements to commercialize public varieties and earnings royalties. A common misconception is that licensing can only happen for PBR-protected varieties, and Nigeria's National Seed Policy 2015 provides guidance for safeguarding inventor efforts through royalties for at least 10 years to help recoup research costs.

source_title: Nigeria Guidebook on Regulatory Aspects of Dissemination of Public Varieties (NML/SFSA/AVISA, 2019)
excerpt_text: Nigeria does not yet have a comprehensive legal framework on Plant Variety Protection (PVP), but the 2019 NASC Act provides that a PVP law shall be put in place based on internationally recognized criteria, and a draft PVP Bill is before the Nigerian House of Representatives which would bring Nigeria's law in line with ARIPO, the Arusha Protocol, the WTO TRIPS Agreement, and ECOWAS. Nigeria is a member of the African Regional Intellectual Property Organization (ARIPO), which adopted the Arusha Protocol for the Protection of New Varieties in July 2015, creating a regional framework for PVP based on the 1991 UPOV Convention; Nigeria is working toward full UPOV membership. A PVP law, once in place, would grant breeders' rights for a minimum of 10 years and would also protect farmers' rights. Despite the public sector developing 87% of varieties released in Nigeria, most seed sector activity still occurs in the informal sector: less than 30% of smallholder farmers use improved seed from the formal sector, while the rest use farmer-saved seed from the informal sector. Increasing access to improved certified seed is important for both food self-sufficiency and regional market opportunities.

source_title: Field insect pests of rice in Africa: biology and control (IITA Research Guide 43, Umeh/Joshi/Ukwungwu, 1995, 2nd ed.)
excerpt_text: Insect pests are a major constraint in rice production in Africa, causing annual crop losses ranging from 30% in upland rice to 100% in lowland rice. About 6.9 million hectares are under rice cultivation in Africa (1992 production ~9.3 million tons); most is grown by resource-poor smallholder farmers averaging only 1.3 tons/ha. Rice insect pests are classified by the plant parts they damage: (1) internal stem feeders (stem borers), (2) leaf feeders, (3) plant suckers (leaf and stem suckers, grain suckers), (4) root feeders. A relationship exists between crop phenology and field infestation of major pests. Control combines cultural, biological, host-plant resistance, and chemical methods, with integrated pest management (IPM) emphasizing keeping populations below the economic threshold (ET); the economic injury level (EIL) is the population causing economic damage.

source_title: Field insect pests of rice in Africa: biology and control (IITA Research Guide 43, Umeh/Joshi/Ukwungwu, 1995, 2nd ed.)
excerpt_text: The African rice gall midge (ARGM), Orseolia oryzivora Harris & Gagne, is a bud borer and one of the most important pests of lowland rice (also now found in uplands). It causes economic damage during vegetative stages (seedling to panicle initiation). Adults are tiny mosquito-like flies ~5 mm long; females have robust orange abdomens, males are smaller with slender brown abdomens and longer antennae. Adults are cryptic and nocturnal, living 2-5 days; females lay 100-200 eggs on leaves, leaf sheaths, ligules and stem bases. Eggs hatch in 2-3 days; larvae creep down leaf sheaths in a film of water and enter buds. Feeding swells the bud and forms a cavity (the gall, also called 'onion leaf' or 'silver shoot'). Each gall represents a tiller lost because tillers with galls do not produce panicles; early/severe infestation causes stunted growth and total crop failure, especially under humid, cloudy conditions. Egg-to-adult development takes 22-30 days; in the dry season a small population survives in ratoons and wild rice.

source_title: Field insect pests of rice in Africa: biology and control (IITA Research Guide 43, Umeh/Joshi/Ukwungwu, 1995, 2nd ed.)
excerpt_text: The stalk-eyed fly (Diopsis longicornis Macquart) is an important pest of lowland rice and also serious in uplands where humidity is high (other African Diopsis include D. apicalis and D. colaris). The head is orange with eyes on reddish stalks; thorax is shiny black with two backward-directed spines and glassy wings. Adults are gregarious and invade nurseries early in the season, laying eggs on leaves and stems of seedlings/transplants. After hatching, maggots move down the leaf sheath and feed on stem tissue below the growing zone, cutting off the apical whorl so the central leaves fail to unfold and dry up — the characteristic 'dead heart' symptom. The larva feeds on healthy tissue then moves forward as the damage spreads; the fully grown larva settles inside the last host tiller to pupate.

source_title: Field insect pests of rice in Africa: biology and control (IITA Research Guide 43, Umeh/Joshi/Ukwungwu, 1995, 2nd ed.)
excerpt_text: Major internal stem feeders (stem borers) include the striped borer (Chilo zacconius), spotted borer (Chilo partellus), white borer (Maliarpha separatella), yellow borer (Scirpophaga sp.), and pink borer (Sesamia calamistis). General damage symptoms of stalk-eyed fly and lepidopterous stem borers are: early dead hearts (tillers with dead inner leaves) in young plants; whole tillers dying as lower stem tissues are eaten; lodging (especially in tall varieties); panicles failing to emerge and drying up; white heads (empty white panicles) when older plants are attacked; improperly filled grains and low-grade grain from borer damage.

source_title: Field insect pests of rice in Africa: biology and control (IITA Research Guide 43, Umeh/Joshi/Ukwungwu, 1995, 2nd ed.)
excerpt_text: Striped borer (Chilo zacconius) is widespread in West Africa and polyphagous on lowland and upland rice from vegetative stage to ripening. Adults are pale yellow with black-spotted forewings and hindwings. Flat pale-yellow eggs are laid in overlapping rows resembling fish scales; first-generation larvae may develop as semi-borers, feeding on leaves/sheaths with pupation in leaf sheaths, and later boring into young stems causing dead hearts. Second-generation larvae cause the main economic damage. Spotted borer (C. partellus) is common in East/Southern Africa and also attacks maize and sorghum; adults have beige forewings (female hindwings white, male straw-coloured). Infestation starts vegetatively; eggs laid in overlapping rows of 50-100 on leaf undersides (up to 300 per female), hatch in ~1 week; larvae feed leaves then penetrate stems causing dead hearts in young plants, mature larvae buff-coloured with longitudinal broken bands, pupate inside the stem.

source_title: Field insect pests of rice in Africa: biology and control (IITA Research Guide 43, Umeh/Joshi/Ukwungwu, 1995, 2nd ed.)
excerpt_text: White borer (Maliarpha separatella) is distributed in East and West Africa and Madagascar; adults are straw-coloured with a prominent brown line on the forewing anterior edge and attack rice at full tillering stage. Yellow borer (Scirpophaga sp.) is common in West Africa; adults have satin-like white wings folded roof-like at rest, black thorax, white legs, and females are slightly larger than males. The yellow borer is a pest of wetlands and attacks new transplants up to the booting stage. Yellow borer eggs are laid on leaves/leaf sheaths; on hatching the caterpillar bores several centimeters below the growing point and eats all internal stem tissues down to the base, destroying the tiller, then cuts a ~4 cm stem section and moves to the next tiller, discarding the old stem tube. Pink borer (Sesamia calamistis) is the most important Sesamia in Africa, more important in upland than lowland rice; adults are light brown with dark-speckled forewings and whitish fringe, strong fliers; eggs laid in batches on leaf sheaths, the pink caterpillar first feeds leaf sheath then bores into stem, older larvae may cut stems completely; panicle attack causes white heads; full-grown larva is 30 mm, pupates at stem base in dried leaf-sheath folds.

source_title: Field insect pests of rice in Africa: biology and control (IITA Research Guide 43, Umeh/Joshi/Ukwungwu, 1995, 2nd ed.)
excerpt_text: Important leaf feeders include caseworm (Nymphula depunctalis), leaf folders (Marasmia sp., Cnaphalocrocis sp.), ladybird beetle (Chilocorus similis), armyworm (Spodoptera sp.), field crickets, and grasshoppers. Caseworm: small whitish moths 6-10 mm with brown-black wing spots; pale yellow spherical eggs laid in batches of 15-20 on leaf undersides touching water surface; on hatching, gregarious first-instar larvae cover themselves with slime and scrape leaf tissues, then each cuts a leaf piece, rolls it into a case sealed with silk, and floats in standing water breathing through thread-like gills — the larva is aquatic and feeds by scraping the leaf underside leaving only papery epidermis. Leaf folders: tiny yellow-brown moths ~5 mm; eggs laid in batches of 2-9, larvae fold leaf edges into a chamber and feed on parenchyma causing longitudinal transparent streaks; badly damaged leaves dry up and fields may appear scorched. Armyworms are occasional but serious pests, more important in uplands; adults migrate long distances and outbreaks follow rains then prolonged drought; green-to-brown larvae with yellowish lines defoliate plants, often leaving only stem bases. Field crickets (long antennae, flattened head) and grasshoppers (short antennae) feed on leaves — crickets leave holes keeping margins intact, grasshoppers eat large edge portions and can wither panicles; both lay eggs in soil pods of 30-100 eggs with frothy coating, and adults attack mature plants.

source_title: Field insect pests of rice in Africa: biology and control (IITA Research Guide 43, Umeh/Joshi/Ukwungwu, 1995, 2nd ed.)
excerpt_text: Plant suckers include leaf and stem suckers (leafhoppers Nephotettix and Corana, planthoppers Nilaparvata/Sogatella/Sogatodes, spittle bugs Locris) and grain suckers (rice bugs Stenocoris, Mirperus, Aspauia, Riptortus, Nezara). Leafhoppers and planthoppers are generally kept below the economic threshold by natural enemies (parasitoids attack eggs, predators attack nymphs and adults); good cultural practices — early planting, early-maturing varieties, weed-free farms, judicious fertilizer use — also suppress them. When populations exceed ET, contact insecticides may be needed. High populations cause 'hopper-burn' — plants wilt and dry. Rice bugs invade fields during flowering and lay eggs on foliage; both adults and nymphs suck developing grains (especially milk and dough stages), sucking the grain empty or producing low-quality grains with brown feeding spots. Rice bugs are long-lived, highly mobile, and can locate isolated farms; control relies on eliminating grassy weeds from fields/bunds/surroundings, avoiding staggered planting, and biological control (parasitoids on eggs, spiders on nymphs/adults, pathogenic fungi), with insecticide spray only when populations reach ET.

source_title: Field insect pests of rice in Africa: biology and control (IITA Research Guide 43, Umeh/Joshi/Ukwungwu, 1995, 2nd ed.)
excerpt_text: Root feeders include termites and mole crickets; they are more important in upland rice and also a problem in irrigated rice if water supply is inadequate. Mole crickets attack both adults and nymphs: they dig shallow tunnels and feed on young roots and basal plant portions below ground, causing wilting and death of plants. Termites attack rice roots causing yellowing and wilting; sometimes stems are cut into small pieces carried into termite galleries for later consumption, and whole plants can die. Control: termites should be controlled at the source (mounds/galleries); locate mounds, poison each with 2.5 tablets of aluminum phosphide (Phostoxin) and seal holes with moist mud; alternatively break mounds and treat with granular carbofuran or drench with chlorpyrifos (or dieldrin where permitted). Seed treatment before planting protects seedlings from termite attack, and carbofuran easily controls mole crickets.

source_title: Field insect pests of rice in Africa: biology and control (IITA Research Guide 43, Umeh/Joshi/Ukwungwu, 1995, 2nd ed.)
excerpt_text: Control of rice pests follows an IPM approach that keeps populations below the economic threshold (ET) using compatible tactics. Cultural control for internal stem feeders includes: using early-maturing varieties and planting early so plants mature before pest build-up; regular weeding to remove alternate hosts; applying moderate fertilizer in split doses over main growth stages to discourage rapid borer development; and destroying rice stubble after harvest to kill diapausing stem-borer larvae (a dry-season non-rice crop also helps). Practices to AVOID because they encourage pest build-up: buying/selling rice seedlings at transplanting markets (seedlings carry hidden infestations); staggered planting across farms (provides continuous food); and panicle harvesting leaving tall stumps (late crops/stubble harbor stem borers over winter). Biological control uses natural enemies (parasitoid wasps, predatory flies/dragonflies/beetles/spiders, mites, and pathogenic fungi); resistant varieties (antixenosis, antibiosis, or tolerance) are an effective but not permanent control because borer resistance tends to break down after several years.

source_title: AgriPadi synthetic compilation - standard Nigerian extension agronomy (crop/season/zone matching)
excerpt_text: Nigeria's rainfall follows a strong south-to-north gradient, and this decides what can be grown and when. The south (rainforest and derived savanna) has a bimodal rainfall pattern: a main rainy season from about March to July, a short dry spell in August often called the 'August break', and a second, shorter rainy season from September to November. This allows two cropping seasons per year for fast crops like maize and vegetables. The Middle Belt (southern and northern Guinea savanna) has one main season, roughly April/May to October. The far north (Sudan and Sahel savanna) has a unimodal pattern: a single short rainy season from about May/June to September/October, giving only 90 to 150 growing days, so only quick-maturing or drought-tolerant crops and varieties can complete their cycle there. Rainfall also becomes less reliable from year to year as you move north. The same crop can therefore have completely different planting windows in the south and the north, and advice that is correct for one zone can be wrong for another.

source_title: FAO GIEWS Country Brief: Nigeria
excerpt_text: Maize planting windows differ sharply across Nigeria because rainfall regimes differ. In southern bimodal-rainfall areas, main-season maize is planted around March to April with the onset of the rains and is harvested between June and August; a second-season crop can then be planted in August/September after the August break, to mature in the second rains. In central areas, sowing generally starts from about mid-April. In northern unimodal areas there is only one season: planting runs from May through July, timed to the onset of the single rainy season. Late planting in the north is risky because the crop may not mature before the rains end in September/October; farmers there should prefer early-maturing varieties if the rains are delayed. Maize is very sensitive to drought at flowering (tasseling and silking): a dry spell of even one to two weeks at that stage, such as the June-to-August dry spells forecast for northern regions, can cut yields heavily. Where a severe mid-season dry spell is expected, sorghum or millet is the safer cereal choice in the north.

source_title: AgriPadi synthetic compilation - standard Nigerian extension agronomy (crop/season/zone matching)
excerpt_text: Sorghum and pearl millet are the cereals best matched to the short, unreliable rainy season of northern Nigeria (Sudan and Sahel savanna). Pearl millet is the most drought-hardy: early varieties mature in about 60 to 90 days, so the crop can escape the end-of-season drought even when the rains stop early, and it yields on poor sandy soils where maize would fail. Sorghum needs a little longer, commonly 100 to 120 days or more, but it tolerates both dry spells and temporary waterlogging better than maize. Both should be planted as soon as the rains are reliably established, usually June to early July in the north; planting sorghum too late in a short season means the grain may not fill before the rains end. If the season starts late, switching from sorghum or maize to an early millet variety is the standard way to still get a harvest. In the south these crops are rarely grown because high humidity and rainfall favour fungal diseases like sooty stripe and grain mould, and bird (quelea) pressure; the humid zone is maize, cassava and yam country instead.

source_title: AgriPadi synthetic compilation - standard Nigerian extension agronomy (crop/season/zone matching)
excerpt_text: Rice fits Nigerian seasons in three different ways. Rainfed lowland rice is planted with the onset of the rains (about May to July depending on zone) into valley bottoms and floodplains that hold water, and is harvested as the rains tail off. Irrigated rice in fadama land and irrigation schemes is grown in the dry season, roughly November to April: the farmer controls the water, so a full second crop is possible in the same year, and the dry, sunny harvest period gives good grain quality. Upland (rainfed) rice depends entirely on well-distributed rainfall and is the most drought-prone system; a two-week dry spell can seriously reduce yield, so upland rice suits the south and Middle Belt with their longer seasons, not the far north. Fadama land - low-lying land along rivers that stays moist after floods recede - is especially valuable in the north because it is the main way to grow rice and vegetables in the long dry season.

source_title: AgriPadi synthetic compilation - standard Nigerian extension agronomy (crop/season/zone matching)
excerpt_text: The best tomato season depends on the region. In northern Nigeria, the main tomato crop is grown in the dry season under irrigation: transplanting around October to November and harvesting roughly December to March. Cooler harmattan-period weather and dry air mean far less fungal and bacterial disease (early and late blight thrive in wet, humid conditions), and dry-season tomatoes often earn better prices because supply from other zones is low. The risk at the end of the dry season (March-May) is heat: temperatures above about 35C at flowering cause flowers to drop and fruits not to set. In the south, tomatoes can be grown in the rainy season without irrigation, but the humid weather brings heavy blight pressure, so the drier second season or the August break period is easier to manage than the peak rains. Wet-season tomatoes anywhere need close disease scouting; irrigated dry-season tomatoes need reliable water and watch for heat at flowering.

source_title: AgriPadi synthetic compilation - standard Nigerian extension agronomy (crop/season/zone matching)
excerpt_text: Cassava is mainly a crop of the south and Middle Belt because it needs a reasonably long moist period to establish, even though an established crop is very drought-tolerant. The best planting time is early in the rainy season, as soon as the soil is moist enough for cuttings to sprout: roughly March to May in the south and around May to June in the Middle Belt. Cuttings planted at the onset establish a full canopy before any mid-season dry spell. Planting too late in the season risks poor sprouting and weak stands when the rains stop. A key advantage of cassava is its flexible harvest: roots can stay in the ground and be harvested any time from about 9 to 18 months after planting, so a household can leave the crop through the dry season and harvest piece by piece. This is why cassava is a food-security backbone in the humid zone. In the short-season far north, cassava is marginal because the single brief rainy season does not give it enough moist months to establish well.

source_title: AgriPadi synthetic compilation - standard Nigerian extension agronomy (crop/season/zone matching)
excerpt_text: Yam needs a long, well-watered growing season of about 7 to 9 months, which is why Nigeria's yam belt is the Middle Belt (Benue, Nasarawa and neighbouring states) and the southern Guinea savanna, with some production into the rainforest zone. Planting is timed to the start of the rains: roughly February to April depending on the zone, so that the long vine growth coincides with the wettest months and tuber bulking happens before the rains end. Deep, loose, well-drained soil matters because tubers rot in waterlogged ground. In the far north, the 90-to-150-day rainy season is simply too short for yam to complete its cycle, so farmers there grow millet, sorghum, groundnut and cowpea instead. A farmer asking whether to plant yam in a short-season zone should be steered to quick crops; a Middle Belt farmer with a long season and good soil is in the best yam country in West Africa.

source_title: AgriPadi synthetic compilation - standard Nigerian extension agronomy (crop/season/zone matching)
excerpt_text: The dry season (roughly November to March, with the dusty, dry harmattan wind from about December to February) does not have to mean no farming: with irrigation or moist valley soils it is a valuable second season. Without irrigation, only harvesting of long-season crops (cassava, yam, late sorghum) and land preparation are realistic, because rainfed planting will fail. With water - fadama valley bottoms, riverbanks, wells, or schemes - the classic dry-season crops are tomato, onion, pepper, leafy vegetables, okra, dry-season rice, and in some northern schemes wheat and sugarcane. Dry-season crops avoid many fungal diseases because the air is dry, but they need reliable water all the way to harvest, and late dry-season heat (March-May) stresses flowering vegetables. Crop residues left after harvest also become the main dry-season feed for goats, sheep and cattle. Farmers should plan water first: choose the crop to match how much water the source can actually deliver for the whole season, and expect better prices for vegetables harvested when rainfed supply is off the market.
